title: 2 Shrinkers
text:
The equation and the associated flow A self-shrinker is a submanifold whose mean curvature flow evolves by dilation toward a fixed center. We use the mean curvature vector convention $\vec H=\Delta_\Sigma X$; for a hypersurface with unit normal $\nu$, this means $\vec H=-H\nu$ and $H=\operatorname{div}_\Sigma\nu$. A normalized $n$-dimensional shrinker in $\mathbb R^N$ satisfies \[
\begin{gathered}\vec H+\frac{X^\perp}{2}=0,\\ M_t=\sqrt{-t}\,\Sigma,\qquad t<0.\end{gathered}
\] Here $\Sigma=M_{-1}$, the center is the origin, and the extinction or singular time is zero. Translation of the center and parabolic rescaling give other normalizations. The vector equation works in every codimension; scalar equations involving one unit normal apply to hypersurfaces. The round spheres , generalized cylinders , and planes through the origin illustrate three different behaviors: collapse to a point, collapse of a spherical factor onto an axis, and stationarity. The subject combines two questions. Which submanifolds solve this elliptic equation? Which of them occur, and persist under perturbation, as singularities of an evolving hypersurface? The introductions of Sun–Wang and Chu–Sun approach the first question through topology and compactness and the second through the dynamics of families of initial surfaces. The distinction is useful throughout this catalogue. Why shrinkers describe singularities To examine a flow near a spacetime point $(x_0,T)$, magnify space by $r^{-1}$ and time by $r^{-2}$. The rescaled flows are \[
M_s^{(r)}=r^{-1}(M_{T+r^2s}-x_0),\qquad s<0.
\] As $r\downarrow0$, compactness permits subsequential weak limits under the usual local mass bounds. Huisken's monotonicity formula forces a tangent flow to be backward self-similar. This is the basic reason for studying shrinkers. The weak conclusion alone does not imply that the profile is smooth, has multiplicity one, or is independent of the chosen sequence; those conclusions require further theorems in the relevant setting. This formulation, recalled in CM12 , Introduction, also explains why shrinkers occur beyond Type I singularities. A different description uses logarithmic time: $\tau=-\log(T-t)$ and $\widetilde M_\tau=(T-t)^{-1/2}(M_t-x_0)$. Then \[
(\partial_\tau X)^\perp=\vec H+\frac{X^\perp}{2}.
\] Shrinkers are precisely the stationary points of this rescaled evolution. Thus convergence toward a singularity becomes a long-time dynamical problem near an equilibrium. A shrinker can have unstable directions and still arise from specially chosen initial data. Conversely, an existence construction for the elliptic equation does not, by itself, show that a general flow approaches that shrinker. Gaussian area, entropy, and stability The natural variational quantity is Gaussian area. For an $n$-dimensional submanifold, define \[
F_{x_0,s}(\Sigma)=(4\pi s)^{-n/2}\int_\Sigma e^{-|X-x_0|^2/(4s)}\,d\mu,\qquad
\lambda(\Sigma)=\sup_{x_0\in\mathbb R^N,\ s>0}F_{x_0,s}(\Sigma).
\] The shrinker equation is the Euler–Lagrange equation for $F_{0,1}$. Entropy allows the Gaussian center and scale to vary, is invariant under translations and dilations, and is nonincreasing along the flows to which monotonicity applies. For a smooth complete embedded normalized self-shrinking hypersurface without boundary and with polynomial area growth, entropy equals $F_{0,1}$. This equality is specific to the shrinker setting; it should not be transferred to a translator or an arbitrary time slice. For a two-sided hypersurface, the linearized rescaled equation and Gaussian second variation involve \[
L f=\Delta_\Sigma f-\frac12\langle X,\nabla_\Sigma f\rangle+\left(|A|^2+\frac12\right)f.
\] For compactly supported normal variations, the fixed-center second variation is $-\int fLf\,(4\pi)^{-n/2}e^{-|X|^2/4}\,d\mu$. Allowing the center and scale to move changes the stability question. Colding–Minicozzi classify the entropy-stable models among smooth complete embedded hypersurface shrinkers without boundary and with polynomial volume growth: the round generalized cylinders, including the sphere and plane. Their $F$-stability classification leaves the sphere and plane. These are distinct statements with distinct variation classes; neither asserts that every shrinker is dynamically attracting ( CM12 , Theorems 0.12 and 0.16). Topology, constructions, and compactness In the plane, the Abresch–Langer family makes the distinction between embedded curves and closed immersed curves essential. In three-space, the Angenent torus shows that embedded shrinkers need not be spherical. Drugan's immersed sphere shows why embeddedness cannot be dropped from genus-zero rigidity: Brendle proves that a compact embedded genus-zero shrinker in $\mathbb R^3$ is round ( CatBrendle2016 , Theorem 1). Rotational ODE methods, gluing of simpler surfaces, and variational min-max arguments lead to quite different constructions. The survey CatDLN2018 , Sections 3–5, explains the role of symmetry; the linked entries below give the hypotheses and topology of individual families. For noncompact surfaces, the geometry at infinity is part of the problem. Under a fixed entropy bound and a fixed finite genus, Sun–Wang prove smooth local sequential compactness for complete embedded shrinkers in $\mathbb R^3$, with the genus preserved in the limit. Their result prevents handles from escaping to infinity; it also gives a uniform bound on the number of ends in terms of genus and entropy. Control of conical and cylindrical ends is central to this argument ( CatSunWang2020 , Theorem 1.1 and Corollaries 1.2–1.3). Local smooth convergence of arbitrary noncompact surfaces would not preserve global topology without such control. Higher codimension brings additional geometry. Products of shrinking spheres give shrinkers of codimension two, including the Clifford torus in $\mathbb R^4$. Sun–Zhu prove that a product of two round shrinking spheres is isolated among sufficiently $C^{2,\alpha}$-close shrinkers, modulo rotations, in any ambient dimension in which it is embedded. Their explicit Łojasiewicz inequalities also quantify convergence near these products ( CatSunZhu2025 , Introduction and Theorem 1.1). This local rigidity is different from entropy stability, and it does not classify all shrinkers of the same topology. From examples to the dynamics of flows Chu–Sun show how topology of a family of initial conditions can force a non-generic singularity. For a smooth path of embedded tori in $\mathbb R^3$ joining the inward-neck and outward-neck pinching behaviors specified in their theorem, some intermediate level-set flow develops a singularity that is neither a multiplicity-one sphere nor a multiplicity-one cylinder. Their analysis produces genus-one singularities and a genus-one shrinker with entropy below a shrinking doughnut ( CatChuSun2025 , Introduction). Robustness here concerns an appropriate family of flows; it is not stability of every individual toroidal shrinker. These results suggest how to use the catalogue: compare topology and ends, then examine entropy, index, and the hypotheses of the relevant rigidity or dynamical result. Existence, uniqueness within a symmetry class, local rigidity, and realization as a singularity answer different questions. The entries are a selection of constructions rather than an exhaustive classification. Their pictures distinguish exact models, numerical ODE solutions, and schematics; topology seen in a drawing does not supply an existence proof.

title: 3 Translators
text:
Translation as a geometric evolution A translator is a submanifold whose mean curvature flow moves with a constant ambient velocity. For a smooth $n$-dimensional submanifold $\Sigma\subset\mathbb R^N$ and a constant vector $V$, the equation and associated flow are \[
\begin{gathered}\vec H=V^\perp,\\ M_t=\Sigma+tV,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.\end{gathered}
\] Only the normal component of the velocity changes the evolving image. We use $\vec H=\Delta_\Sigma X$ and, for hypersurfaces, $\vec H=-H\nu$. After a rotation and a spatial scaling, a nonzero translation velocity can be normalized to $V=e_{n+1}$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The magnitude of the velocity is not preserved by dilation: dilating space by $a>0$ changes the speed to $|V|/a$. The examples below use unit upward translation unless another convention is stated. Translators are eternal solutions, but eternal existence does not imply translation. They are stationary when viewed in a frame moving with $V$. A minimal hypersurface invariant under translation in the $V$ direction is a stationary special case, since $V^\perp=0$. There is no compact boundaryless Euclidean translator with $V\ne0$: the height $h=\langle X,V\rangle$ satisfies $\Delta_\Sigma h=|V^\perp|^2$, so integration on a compact domain would force $\vec H=0$, which is impossible for a compact boundaryless positive-dimensional Euclidean immersion. Type II models and backward limits A finite-time singularity is Type I if $\sup_{M_t}|A|^2\leq C/(T-t)$ near its singular time, and Type II if no such bound holds. In Type II analysis, one magnifies around high-curvature points at their curvature scale. Suitable compactness estimates can produce ancient or eternal limits. Translators are important examples of such limits, but a curvature rescaling alone does not prove that the limit translates. Convexity, noncollapsing, Harnack inequalities, or a classification theorem provide the additional information. The degenerate neckpinches of Angenent–Velázquez provide a concrete link between finite-time singularity formation and translating tip models ( CatAV97 , Introduction). The bowl is particularly important in convex flow. Brendle–Choi prove that every noncompact ancient solution in $\mathbb R^3$ that is strictly convex and uniformly two-sided noncollapsed is a bowl flow, up to scaling and ambient isometries ( CatBrendleChoi19 , Theorem 1.1). Noncollapsing means that interior and exterior tangent balls have radii at least $\alpha/H$ for a uniform $\alpha>0$. Dropping these hypotheses changes the classification problem. The introduction of Sun–Wang emphasizes another connection: a finite-entropy translator can be studied by taking a parabolic limit of its eternal flow as time tends to $-\infty$. Its backward tangent flow is self-shrinking and splits off the translation direction, in the precise weak formulation of their Corollary 2.4. Thus the large-scale geometry of a translator is linked to a shrinker of one lower dimension. This limit may have multiplicity, and the statement does not assert that every translator has a smooth or uniquely determined shrinker profile ( CatSunWang2025 , Sections 1–2). Graphs, weighted minimality, and basic models For unit upward translation, a graph $(x,u(x)+t)$ over a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ satisfies \[
\operatorname{div}\!\left(\frac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}.
\] In dimension one this yields the exact grim reaper $u(x)=-\log\cos x$, with $|x|<\pi/2$. The finite strip width is compatible with completeness because the height diverges at the boundary. In dimensions $n\geq2$, the rotational entire graph $u(x)=f(|x|)$ satisfies \[
\frac{f''}{1+(f')^2}+\frac{n-1}{r}f'=1,\qquad f(0)=f'(0)=0.
\] This regular ODE defines the bowl. Its quadratic leading term, $r^2/(2(n-1))$, describes its growth but does not give the exact surface. Clutterbuck–Schnürer–Schulze establish the profile asymptotics and dynamical stability for graphical initial data whose height difference from the bowl tends to zero at spatial infinity ( CSS07 , Theorem 1.1 and Section 2). A theorem for this asymptotic class is not stability under unrestricted perturbations. Translators are also critical points, for compactly supported variations, of the weighted area \[
\mathcal I_V(\Sigma)=\int_\Sigma e^{\langle V,X\rangle}\,d\mu.
\] Indeed, the first variation in a normal direction $W$ is $\int_\Sigma\langle V^\perp-\vec H,W\rangle e^{\langle V,X\rangle}\,d\mu$. The integral may be infinite on a complete translator; the local variational equation still makes sense. For a hypersurface, the normal Jacobi operator is $\Delta_\Sigma+\langle V^T,\nabla_\Sigma\cdot\rangle+|A|^2$. On a translating graph, the positive vertical normal component provides the stability function. This is weighted stability, distinct from stability for ordinary area or from convergence of the time-dependent flow ( CatHIMWGraphical18 , Section 2). Classification and the range of constructions Hoffman–Ilmanen–Martín–White classify complete translating graphs in $\mathbb R^3$: after normalizing the velocity and allowing the appropriate rigid motions, the possibilities are the bowl, grim-reaper cylinders and their tilted versions, and strictly convex $\Delta$-wings. A $\Delta$-wing exists on each strip of width greater than $\pi$ and is unique up to translation for that width. The theorem concerns graphs over domains perpendicular to the translation direction; it is not a classification of all complete embedded translators ( CatHIMWGraphical18 , Introduction and Theorem 1.1). Outside the graphical class, annular translating catenoids, Scherk-type surfaces, pitchforks, and gluing constructions have different topology and end geometry. The analogy with minimal surfaces is useful because both problems have elliptic variational formulations, but a minimal surface does not become a translator merely by adding a constant velocity. The survey CatHIMWNotes19 explains these constructions and the limits of the analogy. Higher dimensions also admit convex translators beyond the rotational bowl, as in Xu-Jia Wang's work ( CatXJWang11 , Introduction). Dimension, convexity, and graphicality must therefore accompany every uniqueness statement. Prescribing the shrinker at infinity Sun–Wang turn the backward-limit question into a construction. Given a smooth closed embedded shrinker $S^{n-1}\subset\mathbb R^n$ of Gaussian Morse index $I$, they construct an $I$-parameter family of complete embedded translators in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with unique multiplicity-one backward tangent flow $S\times\mathbb R$. The construction is smooth for $n\leq6$; in higher dimensions it allows a singular set of dimension at most $n-7$. The prescribed asymptotics do not determine a unique translator, and their fattening construction gives further nonuniqueness ( CatSunWang2025 , Theorem 1.1 and Section 1.3). For this correspondence, the cross-sectional shrinker and the translator have different dimensions. A genus-one surface in $\mathbb R^3$ supplies asymptotic data for a three-dimensional translator in $\mathbb R^4$; its surface genus is not a genus assigned to the entire translator. Likewise, a backward parabolic limit is different from an unscaled cylindrical end. The catalogue records the precise end description, regularity range, topology, and entropy information for each construction. These distinctions make it possible to compare examples without turning a particular asymptotic classification into a universal one.

title: 4 Expanders
text:
Expansion from a singular initial shape A self-expander is a submanifold whose mean curvature flow evolves by dilation away from a center. With $\vec H=\Delta_\Sigma X$, the normalized equation and flow are \[
\vec H-\frac{X^\perp}{2}=0,\qquad M_t=\sqrt t\,\Sigma,\qquad t>0.
\] The profile is the time-one slice. For a hypersurface with $\vec H=-H\nu$, the scalar equation is $H=-\langle X,\nu\rangle/2$. This sign is opposite to the shrinker equation. A smooth compact boundaryless expander of positive dimension cannot exist in Euclidean space: the identity $\Delta_\Sigma|X|^2=2n+|X^\perp|^2$ contradicts the maximum principle. Planes through the origin are stationary solutions of the expander equation, and nontrivial complete examples are noncompact. The introductions of Bernstein–Wang place expanders at the intersection of two flow problems: emergence from a conical singularity and possible large-time behavior after rescaling. Both concern a scale growing like $\sqrt t$. Unlike reversing a shrinking flow, the expander equation still generates forward mean curvature flow, with area decreasing locally according to the evolution equation. Growth of the whole noncompact image is compatible with this local area decrease. A particularly important class consists of properly embedded hypersurfaces $\Sigma^n\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$ asymptotic to a regular cone $\mathcal C$. Here regular means smooth away from the vertex, and, in a typical $C^k$ formulation, \[
\rho\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal C\quad\text{in }C^k_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})\quad\text{as }\rho\downarrow0.
\] Consequently $\sqrt t\,\Sigma$ approaches $\mathcal C$ away from the vertex as $t\downarrow0$. Prescribing the cone is an analogue of prescribing boundary data at infinity. It does not automatically prescribe the topology of the smoothing or select a unique solution. Asymptotic conicality is an assumption in the results discussed here, not a property asserted for every complete expander. Examples and the meaning of uniqueness The simplest models smooth a planar corner or a graphical round cone. For an expanding graph $\sqrt t\,(x,u(x))$, its time-one height satisfies \[
\operatorname{div}\!\left(\frac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}\right)=\frac{u-x\cdot Du}{2\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}.
\] Reflection or rotational symmetry reduces this to an ODE. The profiles in the catalogue are defined by those equations and their asymptotic conditions, rather than elementary closed formulas. Ding's constructions also address one-sided smoothings of mean-convex cones, with geometric and minimizing hypotheses that are recorded in the relevant entry ( CatDing20 , Sections 4–6). A rotational double cone makes nonuniqueness visible. A disconnected smoothing consists of two graphical sheets, while a connected smoothing can join the two ends through a neck. Their existence ranges depend on the cone angle. Angenent–Ilmanen–Chopp prove a critical-angle picture and also provide numerical investigations; the computed angles should not be mistaken for exact constants ( CatAIC95 , Lemma 2 and Theorem 4). Distinct expanders from one cone give distinct smooth evolutions for positive time with the same conical initial trace. A claim about fattening additionally concerns a specified weak flow: for level-set flow, fattening means that the evolving zero set has nonempty interior. Networks introduce another distinction. A regular planar expanding network solves the curve expander equation on its branches and has three branches meeting at $120$ degrees at each junction. It is not a smooth immersed curve at those junctions. Ilmanen–Neves–Schulze establish uniqueness within a prescribed topological class for regular expanders with the same asymptotic rays; this does not identify different combinatorial types ( CatINS19 , Section 4). The network and hypersurface theories therefore have related equations but different admissible objects. Weighted area and relative expander entropy The expander equation is the stationarity condition, under compactly supported variations, for \[
E(\Sigma)=\int_\Sigma e^{|X|^2/4}\,d\mu.
\] The growing weight makes $E$ infinite on an asymptotically conical expander. Compactly supported first and second variations remain meaningful, but a global comparison requires cancellation at infinity. For a two-sided hypersurface the Jacobi operator is \[
L_E f=\Delta_\Sigma f+\frac12\langle X,\nabla_\Sigma f\rangle+\left(|A|^2-\frac12\right)f.
\] Its quadratic form is $-\int fL_Ef\,e^{|X|^2/4}\,d\mu$ for compactly supported $f$. Stability refers to nonnegativity of this form; in deformation problems at a fixed cone, the permitted behavior at infinity also matters. These conventions should not be confused with the Gaussian weight of a shrinker. Bernstein–Wang develop the relative quantity \[
E_{\mathrm{rel}}(\Gamma,\Sigma)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\left(\int_{\Gamma\cap\overline B_R}e^{|X|^2/4}\,d\mu-\int_{\Sigma\cap\overline B_R}e^{|X|^2/4}\,d\mu\right).
\] The cancellation is a theorem under suitable hypotheses, not a formal subtraction of two infinities. In their two-sided obstacle setting, the reference expanders have the same cone and bound nested domains, and the competing hypersurface bounds a domain between them. The relative limit exists, possibly with value $+\infty$; under the additional $C^2$ asymptotically conical hypothesis in Remark 1.2, it is finite. This framework supports minimization and a forward monotonicity formula ( CatBWRelative2022 , Theorem 1.1 and Remark 1.2). Relative expander entropy is not the translation-and-dilation invariant Gaussian entropy $\lambda$. Deformation, compactness, and degree In CatBWSpace2021 , Theorem 1.1, Bernstein–Wang describe the space of asymptotically conical self-expander embeddings of a fixed model hypersurface, modulo reparametrizations fixing the data at infinity. For $n,k\geq2$ and $0<\alpha<1$, their $C^{k,\alpha}_*$ framework gives a smooth Banach manifold. The map taking an expander to its parametrized cone is Fredholm of index zero. Its derivative has kernel given by normal Jacobi fields that fix the cone. Generic cone data are therefore nondegenerate in the precise sense of that theorem. Nondegeneracy controls local deformations; it is not global uniqueness. Global arguments also need compactness. For surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$, Bernstein–Wang obtain local smooth subsequential convergence when genus and number of ends are fixed and the cone links converge in $C^{k,\alpha}$ to a regular embedded link. They prove corresponding results in the uniformly mean-convex setting, and in low-entropy classes subject to the stated exclusion of low-entropy singular minimal cones ( CatBWCompactness2021 , Theorem 1.1). These hypotheses prevent degeneration; fixing an arbitrary cone alone is not the general compactness theorem. When the cone projection is proper on the domain under consideration, Bernstein–Wang define an integer degree. At a regular cone, it counts preimages with signs $(-1)^{\operatorname{index}}$, rather than simply counting all surfaces. Invariance of this signed count can force additional solutions, including unstable annular expanders for an open set of cones in $\mathbb R^3$ ( CatBWDegree2023 , Introduction and Theorem 1.1). Properness and the chosen domain are indispensable parts of this conclusion. Mountain passes and topological uniqueness The relative variational theory can produce an expander between two others. For $2\leq n\leq6$, let two distinct strictly stable, properly embedded $C^2$-asymptotically conical expanders in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ have the same $C^3$-regular cone and bound nested domains. Bernstein–Wang's mountain-pass theorem produces a third smooth expander between them, with a point in the open intervening region. For generic cone data, it can be chosen unstable. In higher dimensions, their general existence theorem permits a singular set of codimension at least seven ( CatBWMountain2022 , Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2). Thus the dimension range determines whether the variational output is guaranteed to be smooth. Nonuniqueness of surfaces can coexist with uniqueness of topology. For $2\leq n\leq6$ and $k\geq2$, if a $C^{k+1}$-regular cone in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ has entropy strictly below that of $S^{n-1}\times\mathbb R$, all $C^{k+1}$-asymptotically conical self-expanders with that cone are $C^k$ asymptotically conical isotopic with the cone fixed. In particular, they are diffeomorphic; the theorem does not say that they coincide ( CatBWTopology2022 , Theorem 1.1). For these $C^2$-asymptotically conical expanders, Gaussian entropy equals the entropy of the cone, as recalled in that paper's introduction. Neither value is generally the centered Gaussian area of the time-one expander. The resulting questions are geometric as well as analytic: how many smoothings a cone admits, which topologies occur, how solutions change when the cone changes, and which expanders are selected by a given flow. The results above answer substantial parts of these questions under specific hypotheses. The examples below provide concrete entry points into this theory, with dimensions, asymptotic conditions, and numerical limitations stated separately for each family.

title: 5 Other special flows
text:
Time domains and special behavior The preceding chapters organize flows by a symmetry of their evolution. This chapter also includes distinguished solutions characterized by their time interval, asymptotic behavior, or singularity formation. For a smooth immersion $X:M^n\times I\to N^N$, the equation is $(\partial_tX)^\perp=\vec H$, with mean curvature computed in the stated ambient metric. We call a flow ancient if it is defined for every $t<T$ for some finite $T$, immortal if it is defined for all future time, and eternal if it is defined for all real time. These terms describe time domains rather than shapes. Shrinking solitons are ancient, translators are eternal, and expanding solitons exist for every positive time. Ancient and eternal solutions need not be solitons. The grouping here avoids repeating those earlier families and instead emphasizes examples whose shape changes, stationary minimal submanifolds, higher-codimension phenomena, and flows with special finite-time or infinite-time limits. For a smooth closed flow, area satisfies \[
\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Area}(M_t)=-\int_{M_t}|\vec H|^2\,d\mu_t.
\] This dissipation identity explains both the appeal and the difficulty of using mean curvature flow to find minimal submanifolds. Area decreases, but curvature can concentrate, topology can change, and several sheets can converge to the same limiting surface. A stationary limit, when one is obtained with sufficient compactness and vanishing mean curvature, is minimal. Area decrease alone does not provide those hypotheses or guarantee smooth multiplicity-one convergence. Ancient solutions as singularity models Parabolic rescaling about a developing singularity stretches the preceding interval of existence. When the rescaled geometry has the necessary local curvature and mass bounds, a subsequence can converge to a flow defined arbitrarily far backward in time. This produces an ancient model. Fixed-spacetime tangent flows are self-similar by monotonicity; limits obtained by moving the centers and curvature scales can retain non-self-similar ancient dynamics. Distinguishing these limiting procedures prevents the mistaken conclusion that every ancient solution is a shrinker. Convexity provides important rigidity results. Huisken–Sinestrari show, for closed convex ancient hypersurface flows of dimension $n\geq2$ in Euclidean space, that a uniform pinching $h_{ij}\geq\varepsilon H g_{ij}$ with $\varepsilon>0$ forces shrinking spheres. Their equivalent criteria include suitable diameter growth and Type I behavior backward in time ( CatHuiskenSinestrari2015 , Theorem 1.1). Convexity at each time without uniform pinching is a weaker condition and admits richer ancient behavior. The planar Angenent oval makes that behavior explicit. In the normalization used here, it is the closed curve \[
\cos x=e^t\cosh y,\qquad |x|<\pi/2,\qquad t<0.
\] Every slice is embedded, compact, and strictly convex. Its changing aspect ratio rules out evolution by a single dilation. At extinction its rescaled shape approaches a round circle; far backward in time, its upper and lower tips approach oppositely directed grim reapers after translation. Thus one ancient flow connects shrinking and translating models at different scales. The entry derives these limits from the implicit equation and distinguishes it from a graph parametrization ( BV11 , the paperclip solution). For noncompact ancient surfaces, assumptions remain decisive. Brendle–Choi's bowl classification requires strict convexity and uniform two-sided noncollapsing in $\mathbb R^3$ ( CatBrendleChoi19 , Theorem 1.1). It does not classify arbitrary immersed ancient curves, higher-codimension ancient submanifolds, or ancient flows with no curvature restrictions. Higher codimension and changing effective dimension Stryker–Sun's introduction asks how the ambient dimension of an ancient flow is reflected in its backward limit and entropy. Their torus curves give compact ancient curve-shortening flows that span arbitrarily large even-dimensional Euclidean spaces. They explicitly acknowledge the earlier construction of Altschuler–Altschuler–Angenent–Wu ( CatSS19 , Introduction and Remark 1.3; CatAAAW13 , Section 3). These are one-dimensional curves lying on products of circles, rather than surfaces of torus topology. For example, for integers $1=k_1<\cdots<k_m$, their coordinate pairs have the form \[
\bigl(r(t)^{k_j^2}\cos(k_j\theta),\ r(t)^{k_j^2}\sin(k_j\theta)\bigr),\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^m r(t)^{2k_j^2}=-2t,\qquad t<0.
\] The parameter is $\theta\in\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$, the ambient space is $\mathbb R^{2m}$, and the codimension is $2m-1$. The first frequency makes this subfamily embedded. Different coordinate radii dominate at different times: the backward rescaled limit is a circle with multiplicity $k_m$, whereas the extinction limit is a multiplicity-one circle. The full flow nevertheless spans $\mathbb R^{2m}$. This shows why a low-dimensional extinction profile need not capture the ambient dimension of an ancient flow ( CatSS19 , Section 2.1). The related helical examples are noncompact eternal flows. Their radii decrease while the axial coordinate remains fixed, so the pitch-to-radius ratio changes and the evolution is not a homothetic soliton. Every finite-time slice is embedded, but the local limit as $t\to\infty$ is the axis. A three-coordinate projection of a higher-dimensional example can have crossings even when the original submanifold is embedded. The interactive figures therefore distinguish ambient geometry from its display. Stationary solutions and finite-time constructions Every minimal submanifold gives a stationary mean curvature flow. The catenoid is an exact complete properly embedded example in $\mathbb R^3$, with annular topology and two ends. Stationarity does not imply stability: its ordinary area second variation has a negative compactly supported direction, as computed in the entry. Minimal surfaces also serve as barriers and local models in constructions of evolving solutions. Their stability is measured by ordinary area, while the soliton problems in the earlier chapters use different weights. Some special flows are recorded for the singularities they produce. The rotational degenerate neckpinches of Angenent–Velázquez are non-self-similar finite-time solutions with Type II curvature concentration. Their asymptotic analysis involves different spatial scales, including translating behavior near a tip ( CatAV97 , Introduction). Such a construction is an evolving solution of the parabolic equation; an asymptotic profile is not an exact formula for the whole flow. The Whitney sphere gives a different example in higher codimension. It is a Lagrangian immersed sphere in $\mathbb C^n$, $n\geq2$, with a transverse double point. Its symmetric mean curvature evolution collapses in finite time and has a multiplicity-two Lagrangian plane as tangent flow, as established in the setting of Viana's theorem ( CatViana18 , Introduction and Theorem 1.3). The initial immersion has an explicit formula, but the evolution is not self-similar and is not ordinary planar curve shortening of its profile. The ambient codimension and immersion hypothesis are essential to interpreting this example. Immortal flows and multiplicity in the limit Chen–Sun construct a connected embedded rotationally symmetric immortal surface flow in $\mathbb R^3$ whose limit as $t\to\infty$ is a plane with multiplicity two ( CatCS26R3 , Theorem 1.1). The finite-time surfaces are noncompact. Multiplicity two describes the limiting area measure: two sheets contribute mass to the same plane. It does not say that a finite-time slice is a double cover or is nonembedded. The construction concerns an unrescaled infinite-time limit, a different regime from a tangent flow at a finite-time singularity of a closed surface. In a second construction, Chen–Sun obtain compact immortal embedded connected hypersurfaces in $S^n\times[-1,1]$ with the product metric, for every $n\geq2$. They converge to the minimal slice $S^n\times\{0\}$ with multiplicity two. The ambient product region can be included in a closed manifold ( CatCS25Man , Theorem 1.1). This is mean curvature flow in a curved ambient space: it is not the Euclidean evolution of the same hypersurface viewed in a larger vector space. Their introduction uses the example to explain how long-time convergence can lose topology and retain additional mass. These examples organize several recurring questions: what backward and forward limits exist, in which topology they converge, whether convergence is unique, and how dimension, entropy, stability, and embeddedness constrain them. The catalogue answers these questions only where the cited sources do. A closed formula, a prescribed initial immersion, a proven asymptotic model, and a numerical illustration convey different kinds of information, and the entries keep those distinctions visible.

title: 1.1 Sources and conventions
text: MCF-stack collects special solutions of mean curvature flow in four categories: self-shrinkers, translators, self-expanders, and other special flows. This introduction and those four categories form the reading collection. Each example records its equation or construction, source-supported geometric properties, and a picture. Remark 1.1.1 (The source editions) . 912105D5B712 References identify the original papers or the exact supplied editions. Citations distinguish printed page numbers from PDF page numbers and retain original theorem numbers. The source inventory records file hashes and which passages have been checked; an inventoried paper has not necessarily been read. Original PDFs and extracted text are not redistributed. Construction and classification results cited from the literature retain external proofs unless a calculation is supplied here. Remark 1.1.2 (Mean curvature flow and normalization) . 4EDA6AEDEA07 For a smooth immersion $X:M^ n\times I\to \mathbb R^ N$, mean curvature flow is the geometric equation \[  (\partial _ tX)^\perp =\vec H,  \] where $\vec H$ is the trace of the second fundamental form and $\perp $ means normal projection. For hypersurfaces we use $H=\operatorname {div}_ M\nu $ and $\vec H=-H\nu $. Thus the outward normal of a round sphere has positive scalar mean curvature, and the sphere shrinks. title: 2.1 Round shrinking spheres
text: Throughout this collection, the normalized self-shrinker equation is $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and a normalized shrinker $\Sigma $ generates $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $, $-\infty <t<0$. The standard examples appear in [ CM12 ] , pp. 757–759, and [ DLN2018 ] , Section 3.3, PDF p. 8. 5D6AFC4ECF1B For an integer $n\geq 1$, an extinction time $T\in \mathbb R$, and a center $a\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$, the exact family is \[  M_ t=\{ a+\sqrt{2n(T-t)}\, \omega :\omega \in S^ n(1)\} , \qquad -\infty <t<T.  \] The centered normalized slice is $S^ n(\sqrt{2n})$ at $t=-1$. These are smooth compact embedded hypersurfaces without boundary, complete and proper, with topology $S^ n$ and full rotational symmetry. The case $n=1$ is the shrinking circle in the plane. With outward normal and $H=\operatorname {div}\nu $, all principal curvatures are $1/\sqrt{2n(T-t)}$. Thus the flow is strictly convex, $H=\sqrt{n/(2(T-t))}$ and $|A|^2=1/(2(T-t))$. It becomes extinct at $a$ in a Type I singularity at time $T$. The round sphere is entropy stable and $F$-stable, where $F$-stability allows the Gaussian center and scale to vary. These are the stability notions in [ CM12 ] , Theorems 0.12 and 0.16; stability of Gaussian area with center and scale fixed is a different question. The normalized Gaussian integral gives \[  \lambda (S^ n(\sqrt{2n})) =(4\pi )^{-n/2}(2n)^{n/2}e^{-n/2}|S^ n(1)|.  \] In particular, a two-sphere has entropy $4/e$. The three-dimensional picture is the exact surface for $n=2$; for other dimensions a round profile represents the symmetry reduction. 5D6AFC4ECF1B For an integer $n\geq 1$, an extinction time $T\in \mathbb R$, and a center $a\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$, the exact family is \[  M_ t=\{ a+\sqrt{2n(T-t)}\, \omega :\omega \in S^ n(1)\} , \qquad -\infty <t<T.  \] The centered normalized slice is $S^ n(\sqrt{2n})$ at $t=-1$. title: 2.4 Generalized shrinking cylinders
text: The cylinder family is recorded in [ CM12 ] , pp. 758–759. The spherical factor and the number of Euclidean directions are independent discrete parameters. D20709465D01 Let $n\geq 2$ and $1\leq k<n$. In $\mathbb R^{k+1}\times \mathbb R^{n-k}=\mathbb R^{n+1}$ the exact flow is \[  M_ t=S^ k(\sqrt{2k(-t)})\times \mathbb R^{n-k},\qquad -\infty <t<0.  \] Equivalently, $(\omega ,z)\mapsto (\sqrt{2k(-t)}\, \omega ,z)$, with $\omega \in S^ k(1)$ and $z\in \mathbb R^{n-k}$, is a normal parametrization of the flow. These are complete, proper, noncompact embedded hypersurfaces without boundary, with topology $S^ k\times \mathbb R^{n-k}$ and polynomial area growth. Their symmetries include $O(k+1)$ on the spherical factor and all Euclidean isometries in the axial factor. There are $k$ positive principal curvatures $1/\sqrt{2k(-t)}$ and $n-k$ zero principal curvatures. Hence they are mean convex and weakly convex, and $|A|^2=1/(2(-t))$. At time zero the spherical factor collapses onto the axial subspace. Topologically there are two ends if $n-k=1$, and one end if $n-k\geq 2$. Each end has exactly the displayed product geometry. They are entropy stable among the complete embedded hypersurfaces considered by [ CM12 ] , but are not $F$-stable when $1\leq k<n$; see Theorems 0.12 and 0.16. The Euclidean factor leaves entropy unchanged: $\lambda (M_{-1})=\lambda (S^ k(\sqrt{2k}))$. For the round cylinder in $\mathbb R^3$, this is $\sqrt{2\pi /e}$. For $n=2$, $k=1$, an interactive picture displays an exact finite window of the infinite cylinder. End caps are not part of the solution. D20709465D01 Let $n\geq 2$ and $1\leq k<n$. title: 2.2 Planes through the shrinker center
text: Planes are stationary solutions that also satisfy the shrinker equation; see [ DLN2018 ] , Sections 2.5 and 3.3, and [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.16. 97FD822B6630 Let $P$ be an $n$-dimensional linear subspace of $\mathbb R^ N$, where $1\leq n<N$. Then \[  M_ t=P,\qquad -\infty <t<\infty , \qquad \vec H=0,\quad X^\perp =0.  \] Thus $P$ is both a stationary flow and a normalized self-shrinker. An affine plane is a shrinker centered at any point of that plane; it satisfies the centered equation at the origin only if it contains the origin. The inclusion is complete, proper, embedded, flat, noncompact and boundaryless, with topology $\mathbb R^ n$ and Euclidean volume growth. It has two ends for $n=1$ and one end for $n\geq 2$. The solution has no finite singular time. The identity $\sqrt{-t}\, P=P$ does not describe a geometric collapse. Its entropy is exactly one. In codimension one it is entropy stable and $F$-stable under the notions in [ CM12 ] ; no conclusion about a different constrained variation problem is intended. The picture shows a bounded patch of a plane in $\mathbb R^3$. Its boundary is a viewing boundary, not a boundary of the flow. 97FD822B6630 Let $P$ be an $n$-dimensional linear subspace of $\mathbb R^ N$, where $1\leq n<N$. title: 2.3 Abresch–Langer closed shrinking curves
text: The closed planar curves are classified by [ AL1986 ] . The supplied sources record the curvature conservation laws in [ DLN2018 ] , Theorem 1, PDF pp. 5–6, and the rotation-index description in [ CMComplexity2020 ] , Section 6.3, supplied PDF p. 22. 55D5743A6941 Besides the round circle, there are noncircular closed immersed curves $\gamma _{m,\ell }\subset \mathbb R^2$, indexed primitively by coprime positive integers satisfying \[  \frac12<\frac m\ell <\frac1{\sqrt2}.  \] Here $m$ is the rotation index and $\ell $ is the number of periods of the curvature. Their flows are $\sqrt{-t}\, \gamma _{m,\ell }$ for $t<0$. An ODE description in the normalization of this collection is \[  \kappa _{\theta \theta }+\kappa =\frac1{2\kappa },\qquad \kappa >0,\qquad \kappa _\theta ^2+\kappa ^2-\log \kappa =E.  \] Choose the nonconstant periodic solution with curvature period $2\pi m/\ell $. With $T(\theta )=(\cos \theta ,\sin \theta )$ and $N(\theta )=(-\sin \theta ,\cos \theta )$, reconstruction gives \[  X(\theta )=2\kappa _\theta T(\theta )-2\kappa N(\theta ), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb R/(2\pi m\mathbb Z).  \] This is an ODE construction with a closing condition, not a closed elementary formula for $\kappa $. The domain is $S^1$. These are compact, complete, proper immersions with self-intersections. Their curvature is positive after orienting the curve, so they are locally strictly convex; their images do not bound convex embedded domains. The round circle is the only embedded closed shrinking curve. The noncircular curves have finite entropy strictly greater than two, as recorded in [ CMComplexity2020 ] , Section 6.3. The conservation law $\kappa e^{-|X|^2/4}=C>0$ relates curvature to distance from the shrinking center. Compactness makes the shrinking flow a Type I flow becoming extinct at the origin. title: 2.5 Angenent's shrinking torus
text: Angenent constructs an embedded rotational self-shrinker with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$ for each $n\geq 2$ in [ Angenent1992 ] . We use the normalized profile equation from [ DLN2018 ] , Section 3.3 and equation (5.2), PDF pp. 8 and 14. 10374A017921 There is a simple closed profile $s\mapsto (x(s),r(s))$ in $r>0$ whose rotation gives \[  X(s,\omega )=(x(s),r(s)\omega )\in \mathbb R\times \mathbb R^ n, \qquad \omega \in S^{n-1}(1).  \] For Euclidean arclength $s$ and tangent angle $\alpha $, the profile solves \[  x'=\cos \alpha ,\qquad r'=\sin \alpha ,\qquad \alpha '=\left(\frac{n-1}{r}-\frac r2\right)\cos \alpha +\frac x2\sin \alpha .  \] Equivalently, it is a closed geodesic of $r^{2(n-1)}e^{-(x^2+r^2)/2}(dx^2+dr^2)$ on $r>0$. The theorem selects a closed orbit by shooting; the profile is not given by a closed formula. Its flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $, $t<0$. The hypersurface is compact, embedded, complete and proper, with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$, rotational $O(n)$ symmetry and reflection symmetry across $x=0$. When $n=2$ it is a torus in $\mathbb R^3$. It is not mean convex. Indeed, the compact embedded mean-convex classification in [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.17, would force a sphere. It shrinks to the origin with a Type I singularity. It is entropy unstable by [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.12, which applies to this compact embedded non-spherical hypersurface. No exact entropy value or global uniqueness assertion is supplied here. Berchenko–Kogan's numerical calculation estimates its entropy as approximately $1.85122$ ( [ BerchenkoKogan2021 ] , Section 5, PDF pp. 10–12). This estimate has no certified error enclosure; Section 6, Question 6.3, leaves rigorous error bounds open. The proved bound for the separately constructed variational torus is recorded in Example 2.9 . The interactive figure revolves a numerically closed solution of this ODE; its caption records the shooting residual. The profile is not circular. The variational torus in [ DLN2018 ] , Theorem 2, is a separate existence construction; that survey does not identify it with Angenent's torus. 10374A017921 There is a simple closed profile $s\mapsto (x(s),r(s))$ in $r>0$ whose rotation gives \[  X(s,\omega )=(x(s),r(s)\omega )\in \mathbb R\times \mathbb R^ n, \qquad \omega \in S^{n-1}(1).  \] For Euclidean arclength $s$ and tangent angle $\alpha $, the profile solves \[  x'=\cos \alpha ,\qquad r'=\sin \alpha ,\qquad \alpha '=\left(\frac{n-1}{r}-\frac r2\right)\cos \alpha +\frac x2\sin \alpha .  \] Equivalently, it is a closed geodesic of $r^{2(n-1)}e^{-(x^2+r^2)/2}(dx^2+dr^2)$ on $r>0$. title: 2.6 Drugan's immersed shrinking spheres
text: [ Drugan2015 ] , Theorem 1.1, p. 3139, proves the existence of a nonembedded immersed $S^2$ self-shrinker in $\mathbb R^3$. [ DLN2018 ] , Theorem 3, PDF pp. 14–15, gives the corresponding existence statement for $S^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\geq 2$. FE38A115C52C For each $n\geq 2$, there is a smooth rotational immersion $X:S^ n\to \mathbb R^{n+1}$ satisfying $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ whose image is not embedded. The associated immersed flow is $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$, $-\infty <t<0$. In the three-dimensional construction, a graphical piece of the profile, written as axial height $z=\gamma (r)$ for $r>0$, solves \[  \frac{\gamma ''}{1+(\gamma ')^2} =\left(\frac r2-\frac1r\right)\gamma '-\frac\gamma 2.  \] This is equation (1.2) of [ Drugan2015 ] , p. 3140; the paper's radial variable $x$ is denoted here by $r$. Equation (1.3) describes the same curve as a radius depending on height. Shooting and continuation through profile turning points produce the closed immersed sphere; a single graphical piece does not describe the whole surface. The parameter domain is the compact sphere, so the induced metric is complete and the immersion is proper. The image has self-intersections and is not the round sphere. The construction has rotational symmetry and reflection symmetry across a hyperplane perpendicular to the rotation axis. It has no ends. The homothetic flow contracts to the origin with Type I curvature growth. The cited existence argument supplies neither an elementary parametrization nor uniqueness or an exact entropy value. Embedded classification and embedded stability theorems cannot be applied to this immersion by dropping their embeddedness hypothesis. Numerical picture. The picture computes the rotational shooting construction in [ Drugan2015 ] , Sections 2–5, and can be compared with Figure 1 on p. 3141. It shows the two-dimensional immersed sphere in $\mathbb R^3$, not a higher-dimensional projection. Let $s$ be arc length along the meridian and let $\theta $ be its tangent angle measured from the positive radial direction. Substituting $\gamma '=\tan \theta $ into the graph equation gives \[  \frac{dr}{ds}=\cos \theta ,\qquad \frac{dz}{ds}=\sin \theta ,\qquad \frac{d\theta }{ds} =\left(\frac r2-\frac1r\right)\sin \theta -\frac z2\cos \theta .  \] This system continues through the vertical tangents where the graph equation becomes unsuitable for numerical integration. At the upper pole $(r,z)=(0,b)$, smoothness requires $\theta =0$. The even expansion from the graph equation, consistent with Section 6 of the paper, is \[  z(r)=b-\frac b8r^2-\frac{b(b^2+4)}{1024}r^4+O(r^6).  \] We start at $r=10^{-4}$ using this expansion and shoot in $b$ until $z=0$ at the second radial turning point, where $\theta =-3\pi /2$. This is the orthogonal reflection condition in Section 5, pp. 3154–3155. The computation gives \[  b\simeq 0.39345656,\qquad r_{\mathrm{reflection}}\simeq 0.83684239.  \] Reflection across $z=0$, with the order of traversal reversed, completes the meridian from $(0,b)$ to $(0,-b)$. Revolving it gives \[  X(s,\varphi )=(r(s)\cos \varphi ,r(s)\sin \varphi ,z(s)), \qquad 0\leq \varphi <2\pi ,  \] with the angular circles collapsed at the two poles. This is a numerical parametrization at time $t=-1$; the corresponding flow is $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ for $t<0$. The meridian view shows the self-intersections directly. The revolution angle control reveals interior sheets by removing angular sectors; the resulting cut edges are display boundaries, not boundaries of the immersed sphere. The two colors distinguish the shot half from its reflected continuation. The shooting height residual is below $10^{-10}$ before rounding the exported mesh. Halving the initial radius and maximum step and tightening the integration tolerances changes the computed pole height and reflection radius by less than $10^{-9}$. These are floating-point convergence diagnostics, not certified error bounds. In particular, numerical shooting does not prove existence, uniqueness, or that this root is the supremum used in Drugan's proof. text: We follow the supplied June 2020 version of [ ELS2020 ] ; its Sections 2, 4 and 5 distinguish exact geometry, Hamiltonian stability, flow instability and local rigidity. 635FBEF68A7E The exact normalized immersion is \[  X(\theta _1,\theta _2)=\sqrt2 (\cos \theta _1,\sin \theta _1,\cos \theta _2,\sin \theta _2), \qquad (\theta _1,\theta _2)\in (\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^2.  \] It lies in $\mathbb R^4=\mathbb C^2$, and $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ gives a smooth flow for $t<0$. This is a compact embedded Lagrangian torus of dimension two and codimension two, complete and proper. It is minimal in $S^3(2)$ and has the product rotation symmetry $U(1)\times U(1)$. The induced metric is $2(d\theta _1^2+d\theta _2^2)$; it is intrinsically flat, has area $8\pi ^2$, $|\vec H|=1$, and $\vec H=-X/2$. Its entropy is exactly $2\pi /e$ ( [ ELS2020 ] , Section 2 and Lemma 2.4, PDF pp. 3–6). It is $F$-unstable under Lagrangian variations but $F$-stable under Hamiltonian variations after accounting for translations. It is locally volume minimizing under Hamiltonian variations (Lemmas 4.1–4.2 and Theorem 4.3, PDF p. 13). Nevertheless it is not a local entropy minimum, even within Hamiltonian variations. For every $\varepsilon >0$ and $k\in \mathbb N$ there is a compact embedded Lagrangian torus Hamiltonian isotopic and $\varepsilon $-close in $C^ k$ whose first finite-time singularity has a blow-up outside the $U(2)$-orbit of the Clifford torus (Corollary 4.8 and Theorem 4.9, PDF p. 16). A compact embedded two-dimensional self-shrinker in $\mathbb C^2$ sufficiently $C^{2,\alpha }$-close, for $0<\alpha <1$, is the Clifford torus up to translation, dilation and rotation (Theorem 5.7, PDF p. 29). This is a local rigidity statement. The interactive picture rotates the second and fourth coordinates in $\mathbb R^4$ and then projects onto the first three coordinates. Apparent intersections in a projection do not mean that the original torus is immersed nonembedded. 635FBEF68A7E The exact normalized immersion is \[  X(\theta _1,\theta _2)=\sqrt2 (\cos \theta _1,\sin \theta _1,\cos \theta _2,\sin \theta _2), \qquad (\theta _1,\theta _2)\in (\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^2.  \] It lies in $\mathbb R^4=\mathbb C^2$, and $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ gives a smooth flow for $t<0$. This is a compact embedded Lagrangian torus of dimension two and codimension two, complete and proper. It is minimal in $S^3(2)$ and has the product rotation symmetry $U(1)\times U(1)$. The induced metric is $2(d\theta _1^2+d\theta _2^2)$; it is intrinsically flat, has area $8\pi ^2$, $|\vec H|=1$, and $\vec H=-X/2$. Its entropy is exactly $2\pi /e$ ( [ ELS2020 ] , Section 2 and Lemma 2.4, PDF pp. 3–6). It is $F$-unstable under Lagrangian variations but $F$-stable under Hamiltonian variations after accounting for translations. It is locally volume minimizing under Hamiltonian variations (Lemmas 4.1–4.2 and Theorem 4.3, PDF p. 13). Nevertheless it is not a local entropy minimum, even within Hamiltonian variations. For every $\varepsilon >0$ and $k\in \mathbb N$ there is a compact embedded Lagrangian torus Hamiltonian isotopic and $\varepsilon $-close in $C^ k$ whose first finite-time singularity has a blow-up outside the $U(2)$-orbit of the Clifford torus (Corollary 4.8 and Theorem 4.9, PDF p. 16). title: 2.23 Products of closed shrinking curves
text: [ Smoczyk2005 ] , equation (1.4), p. 2984, describes these Lagrangian products. That paper uses $\vec H=-X^\perp $; spatial dilation by $\sqrt2$ converts its examples to the convention used here. AD717A30B415 Let $m\geq 2$ and let each $\gamma _ j:S^1\to \mathbb R^2$ be a normalized closed Abresch–Langer shrinker, including the round circle if desired. Then \[  X(u_1,\ldots ,u_ m) =(\gamma _1(u_1),\ldots ,\gamma _ m(u_ m))\in \mathbb R^{2m}, \qquad (u_1,\ldots ,u_ m)\in (S^1)^ m  \] satisfies $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ for $t<0$. The product formula is exact, but any noncircular factor still requires the curvature ODE and closing condition. The domain is the compact $m$-torus. These are complete proper immersions of dimension and codimension $m$, Lagrangian in $\mathbb C^ m$, with flat normal bundle and nowhere vanishing mean-curvature vector. The product metric is intrinsically flat. A product is embedded when every factor is an embedded circle. A noncircular factor has self-intersections, and so does the product immersion. Multiple covers must not be treated as embeddings. Unless all factor images are circles, the image is not contained in a sphere. The all-circle product in $\mathbb R^4$ is the Clifford torus described separately above. These compact products have no ends and finite entropy. The centered Gaussian integral factors, so $\lambda (\gamma _1\times \cdots \times \gamma _ m)=\prod _ j\lambda (\gamma _ j)$, with the immersion multiplicity counted. They have a Type I homothetic extinction at the origin. No general stability or uniqueness claim for this family is taken from the cited product construction. The figure displays the planar factors and identifies the ambient dimension of their product. title: 2.24 Higher-codimension spherical shrinkers
text: Minimal submanifolds of a round sphere give Euclidean self-shrinkers. This correspondence, and a converse with hypotheses, appear in [ Smoczyk2005 ] , p. 2985 and Theorem 1.1. We use the $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ scaling. 45597E4891F4 Let $n\geq 2$, $N\geq n+2$, and let $F:M^ n\to S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$ be a smooth compact minimal immersion. Viewed in $\mathbb R^ N$, it satisfies \[  \vec H=-\frac12F, \qquad F_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, F,\quad -\infty <t<0.  \] An explicit family is obtained for integers $p,q\geq 1$, $n=p+q$, by \[  F(u,v)=(\sqrt{2p}\, u,\sqrt{2q}\, v), \quad (u,v)\in S^ p(1)\times S^ q(1), \quad N=p+q+2.  \] To avoid repeating the Clifford torus entry, one may take $p+q\geq 3$ in this explicit family. For a general compact minimal immersion, the resulting shrinker is complete and proper; it is embedded when the original immersion is embedded. Topology, symmetry and further curvature properties depend on the chosen minimal submanifold and are not fixed by this construction. Its mean-curvature vector has constant length $\sqrt{n/2}$, and the principal normal $\vec H/|\vec H|$ is parallel in the normal bundle. Conversely, a compact self-shrinker of dimension $n\geq 2$ is spherical if and only if its mean-curvature vector is nowhere zero and its principal normal is parallel (Smoczyk's Theorem 1.1). The displayed product family is compact embedded of Euclidean codimension two, with topology $S^ p\times S^ q$ and $O(p+1)\times O(q+1)$ symmetry. It has $|A|^2=1$ and is minimal inside $S^{n+1}(\sqrt{2n})$; these identities follow directly from its two round factors. For these explicit products, Gaussian factorization gives $\lambda (S^ p(\sqrt{2p})\times S^ q(\sqrt{2q}))=\lambda (S^ p(\sqrt{2p}))\lambda (S^ q(\sqrt{2q}))$. For a general compact minimal immersion $M^ n\subset S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$, $F_{0,1}(M)=(4\pi )^{-n/2}e^{-n/2}\operatorname {Area}(M)$ by the constant radius. The explicit spherical products are locally rigid: for fixed $p,q\geq 1$ and $0<\alpha <1$, a normalized shrinker in $\mathbb R^ N$, $N\geq p+q+2$, sufficiently close in $C^{2,\alpha }$ to the product is an ambient rotation of it. This is [ SunZhu2025 ] , Theorems 1.1–1.2, PDF p. 1. It is a local statement with center and scale fixed, not global uniqueness. The formula determines the product geometry exactly. The figure is a factor diagram with the full ambient dimension stated. 45597E4891F4 Let $n\geq 2$, $N\geq n+2$, and let $F:M^ n\to S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$ be a smooth compact minimal immersion. title: 2.7 Møller closed shrinkers of large even genus

section: 2.7 Møller closed shrinkers of large even genus
text: Møller's construction is stated in [ Moller2014 ] , Theorem 1, and summarized in the supplied [ DLN2018 ] , Section 3.3, PDF pp. 10–11. A105C87CB202 There is an integer $g_0$ such that for every even $g\geq g_0$ there exists a compact smooth embedded orientable surface $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$ satisfying $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$. Its flow is $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g$, $t<0$. This is an existence construction by desingularization, not an explicit formula and not an existence assertion for every positive genus. Each surface is complete and proper, has no ends, and is invariant under a dihedral group of order $2g$. Along the constructed family as $g\to \infty $, the surfaces converge in Hausdorff distance to the union of a round shrinking sphere and a rotational shrinking torus. Convergence is locally smooth away from their two intersection circles ( [ Moller2014 ] , pp. 1–2). The limiting union is singular and is not one of the smooth members. These surfaces are not mean convex and are entropy unstable: apply [ CM12 ] , Theorems 0.17 and 0.12, to the compact embedded non-spherical surfaces. Their homothetic flows have Type I extinction at the origin. The cited construction supplies no exact coordinates or exact entropy value and makes no uniqueness assertion for a specified genus. The illustration follows Figures 1–2 of [ Moller2014 ] : a sphere of radius $2$ intersects a non-circular rotational shrinking torus along two circles. In cylindrical coordinates $(r,\theta ,z)$, the displayed numerical torus meets the sphere near $r=1.783$, $z=\pm 0.906$, consistent with Proposition 2.1. These are numerical coordinates, not exact formulas. Rotation, a quarter cutaway, and a meridian view expose both sheets and the circles where the desingularization takes place. The removed sector is only a viewing aid. As in the paper's Figure 1, this is the singular configuration before handle insertion, not a computed smooth surface $\Sigma _ g$. The second illustration shows how the two intersection circles can be replaced by handles, using gluing schematics of genera $8$, $16$, and $24$. Their mesh topology is checked, but these models do not solve the self-shrinker equation and are not certified approximations to $\Sigma _ g$. The chosen genera illustrate the topology; the cited theorem does not give an explicit $g_0$ that would establish these particular values as members of its constructed family. title: 2.8 Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller shrinkers with one end
text: The original construction is [ KKM2018 ] , Theorem 1.1, arXiv version 3, PDF p. 2. It is among the examples cited in the introduction of [ SunWang2020 ] . A515DF7C7C60 There is an integer $g_0$ such that for every integer $g\geq g_0$ there exists a smooth complete embedded orientable self-shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$, with \[  \vec H=-\frac12X^\perp ,\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g,\quad -\infty <t<0.  \] The construction desingularizes the intersection circle of a plane through the origin and $S^2(2)$. It is a gluing existence theorem; no explicit parametrization of $\Sigma _ g$ is provided. The surface has dimension two and codimension one, is noncompact, has exactly one end, and separates $\mathbb R^3$ into two connected components. Its topology is an orientable closed genus-$g$ surface with one point removed. The compact core and graphical end give properness. It is invariant under the dihedral symmetry group of order $4g+4$ specified in the construction. Outside a ball the end is a graph over a plane, asymptotic to a nonplanar regular cone whose link is a nonzero smooth vertical graph over a great circle of $S^2$. The end has asymptotic height $u(\rho ,\theta )=\rho \sigma (\theta )+O(\rho ^{-1})$; the function $\sigma $ is determined by the construction, not an explicit formula. See equation (1.2), PDF p. 4. As $g\to \infty $, the surfaces converge locally in Hausdorff distance to $S^2(2)\cup P$. The source gives an $O(R/g)$ Hausdorff bound inside $B_ R(0)$; convergence is locally smooth away from the intersection circle. The limiting union is singular, and is not one of the smooth shrinkers. The conical geometry gives quadratic area growth and finite entropy. The source supplies no exact entropy value or numerical entropy bound for individual $g$. It records entropy instability on PDF p. 4. No uniqueness or identification with another construction is asserted. The picture resolves the joining circle using a Scherk-based construction model. The local ingredient in the paper is the singly periodic minimal surface \[  \sinh u\, \sinh v=\sin w,\qquad (u,v,w)\in \mathbb R^3,  \] with period $2\pi $ in $w$; see equation (5.1), PDF p. 9. Section 5 curls $k=g+1$ periods around the equator and attaches the four wings to the upper cap, lower cap, inner disk, and outer sheet. The genus relation is in Remark 5.12, PDF p. 12. The illustration uses a simplified coordinate map and an adjustable conical deformation, not the paper's matched initial surface or the nonlinear correction that solves the shrinker equation. Its cutaway exposes the inner disk and the joining belt. The displayed values $k=6,9,12$ illustrate the topology and do not assert that these genera lie in the theorem's existence range. The outer edge is a display truncation; the waviness is not the computed function $\sigma $. Figure 1 of the paper, PDF p. 3, is itself captioned as a conjectural genus-eight shrinker. title: 2.9 Drugan–Nguyen variational shrinking tori
text: This is the variational construction in [ DruganNguyen2018 ] , Theorem 1, arXiv version 1, PDF p. 1. Its identification with the torus obtained by Angenent's shooting construction is not established in this source. The separate entry records the proved Gaussian-area bound, without claiming that the two constructions give distinct surfaces. 9F3C76F8391F For every integer $n\geq 2$, the weighted half-plane $\{ (r,x):r>0\} $ with metric \[  g_ n=r^{2(n-1)}e^{-(r^2+x^2)/2}(dr^2+dx^2)  \] contains a simple closed geodesic $\gamma _ n=(r,x)$ whose weighted length satisfies \[  L_{g_ n}(\gamma _ n)<2\int _0^\infty s^{n-1}e^{-s^2/4}\, ds.  \] Revolving this curve gives a normalized self-shrinker \[  X(u,\omega )=(r(u)\omega ,x(u)),\qquad (u,\omega )\in S^1\times S^{n-1}(1), \qquad \vec H=-X^\perp /2.  \] The profile is obtained by a variational and modified curve-flow argument, not by a closed formula. The smooth MCF is $\sqrt{-t}\, X$, $t<0$. This is a compact embedded hypersurface of dimension $n$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$ and rotational $O(n)$ symmetry. It is complete, proper, boundaryless and has no ends. For $n=2$ it is an embedded genus-one torus in $\mathbb R^3$. The rotational Gaussian integral and the length bound give \[  \lambda (\mathcal T_ n)=F_{0,1}(\mathcal T_ n) =(4\pi )^{-n/2}|S^{n-1}(1)|L_{g_ n}(\gamma _ n)<2.  \] Thus this family has a proved entropy upper bound in every stated dimension. The theorem does not provide an exact entropy value. In dimension two, this is the shrinking doughnut $\mathcal T$ used by [ ChuSun2025 ] , Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.7, to produce genus-one singularities and an embedded genus-one shrinker of strictly lower entropy. That conclusion does not identify the lower-entropy model with a particular previously constructed family. The asserted bound is attached to this variationally constructed torus. A numerical value for the Angenent shooting profile is a different type of evidence and does not establish that the profiles coincide. The illustration shows the weighted half-plane construction and a clearly labelled torus topology schematic. title: 2.10 Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz shrinkers of every positive genus

section: 2.10 Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz shrinkers of every positive genus
text: [ BNS2025 ] , Theorems 1.2–1.3, arXiv version 2, PDF p. 2, establish this family by equivariant min-max methods. The family is discussed in [ ChuSun2025 ] , Remark 1.5. 40F2B3444C2E For every integer $g\geq 1$ there exists a complete embedded noncompact self-shrinker $\Theta _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$. The smooth flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Theta _ g$ for $t<0$, using $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$. There is no explicit parametrization. These surfaces have dimension two and codimension one, are proper and boundaryless, and have a finite number of annular ends. Properness and the end topology are recorded in Corollary 2.8, PDF p. 8. They have at least one asymptotically conical end. Any additional ends are asymptotically conical or cylindrical. The proved symmetry is invariance under the dihedral group $D_{g+1}$ of order $2(g+1)$, generated by half-turns about $g+1$ horizontal axes. The surface contains these axes and meets the vertical axis orthogonally. Additional reflection symmetry is proposed, rather than proved, in Section 2, PDF pp. 3–4. For all sufficiently large $g$, there is exactly one asymptotically conical end. As $g\to \infty $, $\Theta _ g$ converges as a varifold to the union of the horizontal plane and $S^2(2)$, smoothly locally away from their intersection circle. Theorem 1.3 does not establish exactly one end for every small genus. The normalized Gaussian area satisfies the proved bound \[  1<F_{0,1}(\Theta _ g)\leq 1.02+\frac4e<3.  \] This is Lemmas 2.5–2.6, PDF p. 7: the multiplicity is one and $F_{0,1}(\Theta _ g)$ equals the min-max width. For these normalized complete shrinkers, Gaussian area equals entropy. The numerical simulation for $g=1$ gives Gaussian area approximately $1.7143$ (Section 4, Table 1, PDF p. 15). It is not a certified value for a uniquely identified min-max surface. The source conjectures that $\Theta _1$ has lower entropy than the Angenent torus and Gaussian Morse index five; neither statement is its existence theorem. The relation between the large-genus members and the Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller construction is not proved to be equality. The interactive illustration is an original topology schematic informed by Section 4, Figures 3–4, PDF pp. 14–15, not a numerical solution of the shrinker equation. A vertical cutaway reveals the central sheet and lower cap. title: 2.11 Ketover self-shrinking doubled planes
text: The following is [ Ketover2024 ] , Theorem 1.1, arXiv version 2, PDF pp. 2–3. The construction is variational, with genus determined in Section 6 and the ends analyzed in Section 8. 9E9A8A1CC506 For every integer $g\geq 1$ there exists an embedded self-shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$ such that \[  \lambda (\Sigma _ g)=F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ g)<2, \qquad \lim _{g\to \infty }\lambda (\Sigma _ g)=2.  \] The normalized smooth flow is $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g$, $t<0$. There is no explicit formula for $\Sigma _ g$. The construction gives a smooth complete properly embedded boundaryless surface of dimension two and codimension one. It is invariant under the prismatic group $D_{g+1}\times \mathbb Z_2$, including reflection across the horizontal plane $P=\{ z=0\} $. The group has order $4(g+1)$. For all sufficiently large $g$, the surface is noncompact with exactly two asymptotically conical ends: one in $z>0$ and one in $z<0$, each graphical over the exterior of a disk in $P$. Their cone links converge in $C^0$ to the equator as $g\to \infty $. For these $g$, the topology is a closed orientable genus-$g$ surface with two points removed. For the small-genus members, this theorem does not establish noncompactness or an exact number of ends. Numerical evidence for two ends already at $g=1$ is stated separately in Remark 1.2. As $g\to \infty $, $\Sigma _ g\to 2P$ as varifolds. From every subsequence one can extract a further subsequence and find a radius $r>0$ such that the surfaces are two normal graphs converging smoothly on each compact subset of $P\setminus C_ r$, where $C_ r=\{ (x,y,0):x^2+y^2=r^2\} $. The radius is part of the subsequential conclusion, not a prescribed geometric parameter. For sufficiently large $g$, the level set flow starting from the smooth surface $\Sigma _ g$ fattens (Theorem 1.3, PDF p. 4). The homothetic flow reaches its asymptotic cone at time zero; this statement concerns weak continuation beyond that singular time. Entropy minimization among genus-$g$ shrinkers is conjectural (Remark 1.2). Neither uniqueness nor a particular value below two is claimed. The interactive picture is an original topology schematic informed by Proposition 7.4 (PDF pp. 36–37) and Section 8. The round waists, neck sizes, circle radius and cone slopes are illustrative, not computed geometry. title: 2.12 Closed shrinkers from spherical doubling
text: 826D61792601 For every sufficiently large integer $m$, Kapouleas–McGrath construct a smooth closed embedded surface $S_ m\subset \mathbb R^3$ by doubling the round self-shrinking sphere $S^2(2)$. In the two-latitude subfamily, two nearby sphere sheets are joined by $2m$ small catenoidal bridges, with $m$ bridge sites on each of two latitude circles. The resulting surface satisfies \[  \vec H_{S_ m}=-\frac{X^\perp }{2},\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, S_ m,\quad -\infty <t<0.  \] The formula specifies the evolution after the existence construction; it is not an explicit formula for $S_ m$. The surface has dimension two and codimension one. It is connected, orientable, compact without boundary, smoothly embedded, complete and proper. Its genus is $g=2m-1$, and it has no topological ends. This statement is the specialization $k_\circ =2$ and $\mathbf m=(m)$ of the construction. The threshold for sufficiently large $m$ is not made effective here. It does not supply all small genera. The selected surfaces are invariant under $\mathcal G_ m=D_{2m}\times \mathbb Z_2$, of order $4m$, where $D_{2m}$ denotes a dihedral group of order $2m$. This is an asserted symmetry subgroup, not a classification of the entire isometry group. As $m\to \infty $, the surfaces converge as varifolds to the radius-two sphere with multiplicity two. Each member before the limit is a smooth embedded connected surface; the doubled sphere is the limiting configuration. Since $S_ m$ is a centered shrinker, its entropy equals its normalized Gaussian area. The area inequality in the Gaussian metric $g=e^{-|x|^2/4}g_{\rm Euc}$ gives \[  \lambda (S_ m)=F(S_ m)=\frac1{4\pi }\int _{S_ m}e^{-|x|^2/4}\, d\mathcal H^2 <2F(S^2(2))=\frac8e.  \] This is a rigorous bound obtained from the gluing theorem, not a numerical entropy computation. An individual numerical entropy, the exact Gaussian Morse index, and a uniqueness classification are not recorded by this entry. The spherical input has the required trivial Jacobi kernel, verified directly in Section 10 of the source. This specialization does not rely on the separate theorem on doubling the Angenent torus. See [ KapouleasMcGrath2023 ] , arXiv version 4: Theorem 10.5 (PDF page 66), Theorem 9.40 (page 65), Definitions 7.10–7.11 and Remark 7.12 (page 40), and Theorem 5.7 with equation (5.9) (page 30; also Theorem A on page 3). Its latitude placement uses a numerical balanced linearized guide from equation (10.3) and Definitions 7.24 and 7.29; the neck sizes and sheet separation are enlarged for visibility. The displayed values of $m$ illustrate the topology but are not asserted to lie in the existence range. title: 2.13 Nguyen's one-ended shrinking saddles
text: B28BB2912147 For every sufficiently large integer $m$, Nguyen constructs a smooth complete embedded surface $\widetilde M_ m\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $m-1$, with one asymptotically conical end. The source uses \[  \mathbf H_{\widetilde M_ m}=-\widetilde X^\perp .  \] Thus the catalogue's normalized example is $M_ m=\sqrt{2}\, \widetilde M_ m$, which satisfies $\mathbf H=-X^\perp /2$, and its flow is $M_ m(t)=\sqrt{-t}\, M_ m$ for $t<0$. The construction replaces the intersection circle of a sphere and a plane by a bent, scaled singly periodic Scherk surface, then solves the nonlinear shrinker equation by a perturbation argument. In the catalogue normalization the input sphere has radius $2$. This is an existence construction, with no closed parametrization of the completed shrinker. Its proved properties and construction data include the following. The surface has dimension two and codimension one. It is connected, orientable, noncompact, proper, and without boundary. Outside a compact set it is a graph over the exterior of a planar disk. Consequently it has one topological end; the asymptotic cone is not an assertion that the end is planar. The $m$ periods of the Scherk piece produce genus $m-1$. The existence theorem requires $m$ sufficiently large and does not establish the small-$m$ cases. The surface is invariant under a half-turn about the $x$-axis and under reflections in vertical planes making angles $\pi /(2m)+j\pi /m$, $j\in \mathbb Z$, with that axis. These are finite symmetries, not full rotational symmetry. As $m\to \infty $, the source proves convergence to the spherical input on compact subsets of the upper half-ball in Theorem 1(iv), and convergence to the singly periodic Scherk model after translating and rescaling the joining region in Theorem 1(vi). These limits describe different spatial scales. The conical graphical end gives quadratic area growth and finite entropy. In the stated normalization $F_{0,1}(M_ m)=\lambda (M_ m)$; no scalar entropy value or uniform numerical bound is recorded here. The theorem does not give a global uniqueness or stability classification. Source: [ NguyenShrinker2014 ] , Theorem 1 and its preceding topology paragraph, PDF p. 2; the construction of the outer graphical piece and Proposition 14, PDF p. 13; Definition 21, PDF p. 20; the final fixed-point argument, PDF pp. 24–25. This is another sphere–plane desingularization construction beside Example 2.8 ; no identification or noncongruence between the two families is asserted. The interactive construction schematic shows a connected saddle belt, with a cutaway exposing the inner disk and lower cap. Its unwrapped view triangulates the exact minimal ingredient \[  \Sigma _0=\{ (x,y,z)\in \mathbb R^3:\sin y=\sinh x\, \sinh z\} ,  \] which has period $2\pi $ in the $y$-direction (Section 2, PDF p. 7). The four wings attach to the two caps, the inner disk, and the exterior sheet (Definition 13, PDF p. 13). The global drawing uses an illustrative wrapping and cap map, with a freely chosen conical profile; it does not compute the source's unbalancing parameter, matched rotational caps, or nonlinear correction. The displayed period counts are not asserted to lie in the existence range. title: 2.25 Angenent torus cylinders
text: FA65887C28F1 Let $T^2\subset \mathbb R^3$ be a normalized embedded Angenent shrinking torus as in Example 2.5 . For every integer $k\geq 1$, its Euclidean product \[  \Sigma _ k=T^2\times \mathbb R^ k\subset \mathbb R^{k+3}  \] is a smooth embedded shrinker of dimension $k+2$ and codimension one. If $X_ T(p)$ parametrizes the torus, the exact product and flow formulas are \[  X(p,z)=(X_ T(p),z),\qquad \Sigma _ k(t)=\sqrt{-t}\, T^2\times \mathbb R^ k,\quad t<0.  \] The torus factor itself is specified by its closed weighted geodesic or rotational ODE, not by a closed elementary formula. Since the Euclidean factor is tangent to the product, \[  \mathbf H_{\Sigma _ k}=(\mathbf H_ T,0)=-\tfrac 12(X_ T^\perp ,0) =-\tfrac 12X^\perp .  \] This verifies the product construction directly. Each product is connected, complete, proper, noncompact, and without boundary, with topology $T^2\times \mathbb R^ k$. It has two topological ends when $k=1$ and one when $k\geq 2$. Its intrinsic dimension is at least three, so a surface genus is not assigned; genus one describes the torus factor only. The product inherits the torus's axial rotational symmetry and is invariant under translations and orthogonal transformations in the Euclidean factor. The two ends of $\Sigma _1\subset \mathbb R^4$ have the fixed torus as cross-section. Gaussian integration in the Euclidean factor gives, for $a\in \mathbb R^3$, $b\in \mathbb R^ k$, and $\tau >0$, \[  F_{(a,b),\tau }(\Sigma _ k)=F_{a,\tau }(T^2),\qquad \lambda (\Sigma _ k)=\lambda (T^2)=F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ k).  \] Indeed, the extra factor is $(4\pi \tau )^{-k/2}\int _{\mathbb R^ k}e^{-|z-b|^2/(4\tau )}\, dz=1$. Thus the numerical estimate $1.85122$ for the torus also estimates these products, with the same lack of a certified error enclosure; the product identity itself is exact. As Euclidean products of a closed nonflat embedded shrinker, these examples fall within the realization theorem of [ CLSZ2026 ] , Theorem 1.2, PDF p. 2: each can occur with multiplicity one as a first-singularity tangent flow of a closed embedded hypersurface in the corresponding Euclidean space. The theorem does not assert that the initial closed hypersurface is this noncompact product. The factor is constructed in [ Angenent1992 ] ; the numerical entropy estimate is [ BerchenkoKogan2021 ] , Section 5, with its error-bound limitation in Section 6. The interactive picture shows only three $z$-slices of $\Sigma _1$ after projection from $\mathbb R^4$ to $\mathbb R^3$. It uses the catalogue's numerical torus mesh. Apparent intersections are projection artifacts; the three slices do not represent three components or the entire three-dimensional hypersurface.
