title: 2.14 Ilmanen–White two-ended shrinkers
text: 4522A41972E4 For every integer $h\geq 2$, Ilmanen–White construct a smooth complete properly embedded self-shrinking surface $\Sigma _ h\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $h$ with exactly two ends. In their notation the initial wheel has genus $g=h+1$ and its tangent shrinker has genus $g-1$. The normalized flow is \[  \vec H=-X^\perp /2,\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ h,\quad t<0.  \] There is no explicit formula: $\Sigma _ h$ is obtained as a tangent flow of a critical wheel. This is a connected orientable noncompact surface, of dimension two and codimension one, with topology a closed genus-$h$ surface with two punctures. Both ends are smoothly asymptotically conical. The part above $P=\{ z=0\} $ is a graph over the unbounded component of $P\setminus \Sigma _ h$; the lower part is its reflection. The intersection with $P$ consists of $h+1$ disjoint smooth closed curves. Its symmetries include reflection in $P$, reflections in the vertical planes at angles $j\pi /(h+1)$, and rotation through $2\pi /(h+1)$ about the vertical axis. The two cone links lie on opposite sides of the equator. The authors construct a compact embedded initial surface of genus $h+1$ whose first singular time has exactly one singular point and this multiplicity-one tangent shrinker. Corollary 4.11 gives uniqueness of the tangent flow at that point, not uniqueness of all shrinkers with these topological data. As $h\to \infty $, the shrinkers converge as varifolds to $2P$. After passage to a subsequence, convergence is smooth with multiplicity two away from one circle in $P$. For sufficiently large $h$, the initial compact wheel fattens immediately after its first singular time. No effective genus threshold for fattening is given. The conical ends imply quadratic area growth and finite entropy, with $\lambda (\Sigma _ h)=F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ h)$. An exact value or a numerical upper bound for this particular construction is not recorded here. In particular, the entropy bound for Ketover's construction is not transferred to this one. See [ IlmanenWhite2025 ] , version 3: Theorem 1.1 (PDF p. 2), Theorem 4.8 and Corollaries 4.9 and 4.11 (pp. 10–12), Theorem 7.6 (pp. 20–21), Theorem 9.4 (p. 26), and Theorem 10.5 (p. 31). The paper leaves open whether these shrinkers coincide with Ketover's doubled-plane examples. The interactive illustration follows the upper-graph and reflection description, with $h+1$ equatorial neck curves and two flaring ends. Its default genus $h=3$ matches the topology of Figure 1 (credited there to David Chopp); it does not reproduce Chopp's numerical surface. Neck shapes, lengths, and cone slopes are illustrative, and the shrinker equation has not been solved. section: 2.15 Shao–Zou shrinkers with any prescribed number of ends
text: 4BFAC8529BEA (Shao–Zou plane stackings) Fix an integer $k\geq 2$. For every sufficiently large integer $m$, with the threshold allowed to depend on $k$, Shao–Zou construct an embedded self-shrinker $\Sigma _{k,m}\subset \mathbb R^3$ with \[  \operatorname {genus}(\Sigma _{k,m})=(k-1)(m-1),\qquad \# \operatorname {ends}(\Sigma _{k,m})=k, \qquad \vec H=-X^\perp /2.  \] Their parameter is $J=(k-1)/2$. The smooth flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _{k,m}$ for $t<0$. The surface is obtained by elliptic gluing, rather than an explicit parametrization. The construction stacks $k$ perturbations of the horizontal plane and connects each consecutive pair by $m$ catenoidal bridges. Thus there are $(k-1)m$ bridges in total, placed on alternating equally spaced neck configurations whose radii approach the same balanced radius. Consecutive configurations have angular offset $\pi /m$ (Definition 4.3 and equations (5.15), (5.23)). The compact core and graphical ends give a connected, orientable, complete, proper, boundaryless noncompact surface. Each of the $k$ annular ends is asymptotic to a cone. Theorem 8.1 gives the leading cone slopes in terms of the solved bridge parameters with error estimates; these asymptotic expressions are not formulas for the whole shrinker. For even $k$, the asserted symmetry is the $m$-gonal prism group $D_{mh}$; for odd $k$, it is the $m$-gonal antiprism group $D_{md}$. Both have order $4m$. Horizontal reflection is a symmetry in the even-$k$ case and is not an element of the stated antiprism group in the odd-$k$ case. For fixed $k$ and $m\to \infty $, $\Sigma _{k,m}$ converges as a varifold to the horizontal plane with multiplicity $k$. Each surface before the limit is embedded with multiplicity one. The limiting plane is not a smooth member of the positive-genus family. Conical ends imply quadratic area growth and finite entropy, and $F_{0,1}(\Sigma _{k,m})=\lambda (\Sigma _{k,m})$. No exact value or numerical entropy upper bound is asserted here. A local varifold limit alone is not used to assign a numerical entropy limit. The source expects its $k=2$ and $k=3$ examples to agree with earlier doubled- and tripled-plane constructions when the parameters overlap, but it does not prove those identifications. It supplies no uniqueness or exact Morse-index classification. See [ ShaoZou2025 ] , version 1: the introductory theorem (PDF p. 2), Definition 2.28 and Remark 2.29 (p. 7), and Theorem 8.1 (pp. 31–32). title: 2.16 Flow-generated Platonic and polygonal shrinkers
text: A455BCCC51D0 (Hoffman–Martin–White ray-avoiding shrinkers) Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^3$ be the union of rays from the origin through either the face centers of a regular Platonic solid or the vertices of a regular horizontal $n$-gon, $n\geq 3$. If $q$ is the number of rays, Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ Q$ of genus $q-1$ such that \[  \Sigma _ Q\cap Q=\varnothing ,\qquad \vec H_{\Sigma _ Q}=-X^\perp /2.  \] The associated smooth flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ Q$, $t<0$. This is a construction through singularities of mean curvature flow, not an explicit formula. The surface has dimension two and codimension one, is complete, proper, orientable and without boundary, and has all symmetries of $Q$. The genera are $3,5,7,11,19$ for the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron respectively. For the regular $n$-gon the genus is $n-1$. It occurs with multiplicity one as a tangent shrinker of an initially compact, smoothly embedded surface in $\mathbb R^3\setminus Q$. This realization statement is part of the construction, rather than an identification with Ketover's min-max surface. The theorem does not determine compactness or the number and types of ends for the Platonic examples or the small-$n$ polygonal examples. The discussion after the theorem states that the polygonal examples are noncompact for sufficiently large $n$ and converge to a multiplicity-two plane as $n\to \infty $; it does not give an exact end count there. Each example has finite entropy as a tangent shrinker of a compact initial flow, and $\lambda (\Sigma _ Q)=F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ Q)$. No numerical entropy bound or exact value is recorded here. No uniqueness or equality with the corresponding Ketover or Ilmanen–White constructions is asserted. See [ HMW2026 ] , version 3: Theorem 12 and its discussion (PDF pp. 8–9), with the multiplicity-one tangent-flow convention on p. 4. The compact numerical pictures mentioned in the paper do not establish compactness of the members selected by the theorem. The illustration is an original compact topology model inspired by the construction of initial surfaces in Theorem 24 (PDF pp. 15–16): a thickened spherical edge skeleton has one passage around each ray of $Q$. In the polygonal case the skeleton consists of $n$ meridian semicircles joining the poles, midway between the excluded rays. The inner and outer walls join around the passages, giving genus $q-1$. The cutaway exposes this cavity. These models are not computed shrinkers or simulated flow slices; their compactness is not a claim about the tangent shrinkers. The cubical silhouette also recalls Chopp's numerical picture in Figure 2, without reproducing its mesh. title: 2.17 Flow-generated sphere–plane shrinkers
text: 45B364E949D5 (Hoffman–Martin–White sphere–plane family) Write $d_1=\sqrt{2\pi /e}$ and $d_2=4/e$. For every integer $g\geq 1$ and every fixed \[  1+d_2<\delta <1+d_1,  \] Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$ with $\lambda (\Sigma _ g)<\delta $. They produce it as a tangent shrinker of an intrinsically flowing compact surface in $S^2\times \mathbb R$; the tangent shrinker itself is Euclidean. It satisfies $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, with homothetic flow $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g$ for $t<0$. No explicit parametrization is known from this construction. This is a connected, orientable, complete, properly embedded surface of dimension two and codimension one. It contains the union $Q_ g$ of $g+1$ horizontal lines through the origin at angles $j\pi /(g+1)$, and $\Sigma _ g\cap \{ z=0\} =Q_ g$. In particular it is noncompact. Its complement of the horizontal plane has genus zero. The symmetry group $G_ g$ used here is generated by reflection in vertical planes at angles $(2j+1)\pi /(2(g+1))$, rotations about the vertical axis through $2\pi /(g+1)$, and half-turns about the lines in $Q_ g$. This is the Costa–Hoffman–Meeks symmetry group specified in Section 5. For all sufficiently large $g$, $\Sigma _ g$ has exactly one asymptotically conical end. For small $g$, the theorem does not specify an exact number of ends. For a fixed admissible $\delta $, as $g\to \infty $ the surfaces converge to $\{ z=0\} \cup S^2(2)$, smoothly with multiplicity one away from the equatorial intersection circle. The normalized Gaussian area equals entropy and obeys \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ g)=\lambda (\Sigma _ g)<\delta <1+\sqrt{2\pi /e}<3.  \] The choice of $\delta $ is part of the existence statement; it does not assign an exact entropy to a fixed uniquely determined member. No identification with the Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz min-max examples or the Kapouleas–Kleene–Moller and Nguyen gluing examples is proved. The shared topology and limiting configuration do not establish that they coincide or are distinct. See [ HMW2026 ] , version 3: Section 5 (PDF pp. 16–17), Theorems 40–42 (pp. 26–31), Section 9 (p. 40), and Lemma 64 (pp. 45–46). The source uses $\leq \delta $ in Theorem 40; the strict bound above is its refined choice in Theorem 41. title: 2.18 Flow-generated three-ended shrinkers
text: 5CED6ED3B586 (Hoffman–Martin–White three-ended family) For every sufficiently large integer $g$, Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ with genus $2g$ and exactly three ends. It has the normalization and smooth evolution \[  \vec H=-X^\perp /2,\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g,\quad t<0.  \] The construction obtains the surface as a multiplicity-one tangent shrinker of a flow whose initial surface is compact and embedded in $S^2\times \mathbb R$ with its product metric. The shrinker lives in the Euclidean tangent space. There is no explicit parametrization. It is a connected, orientable, complete, proper noncompact surface of dimension two and codimension one. Its topology is a closed genus-$2g$ surface with three punctures; the three ends are annular and asymptotically conical. It has the group $G_ g$ and the union of lines $Q_ g$ specified in Example 2.17 . In particular, $\Sigma _ g\cap \{ z=0\} =Q_ g$ and $\Sigma _ g\setminus \{ z=0\} $ has genus zero. These are the symmetries of the genus-$g$ Costa–Hoffman–Meeks minimal surface, but the shrinker has genus $2g$. As $g\to \infty $, the surfaces converge to the horizontal plane with multiplicity three. After passage to a subsequence, convergence is smooth away from one circle in that plane. The circle is part of the limiting analysis, not an independently prescribed radius. The entropy has a bound $\lambda (\Sigma _ g)\leq \Lambda <\infty $ independent of $g$, and $F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ g)=\lambda (\Sigma _ g)$. The paper does not specify a numerical value of $\Lambda $ in this theorem. This entry therefore does not assert $\lambda <3$ or an exact entropy limit. For each small $g$ the preceding construction produces a shrinker with genus $g$ or $2g$ and a uniform entropy bound; the assertions of genus $2g$ and three ends require $g$ sufficiently large. The paper's genus-two picture is explicitly conjectural and is not a numerical approximation. No uniqueness or identification with Shao–Zou's tripling construction is proved. See [ HMW2026 ] , version 3: Theorem 43 (PDF p. 31), Theorem 55 and Conjecture 56 (p. 38), Theorem 59 (p. 39), Proposition 62 and Lemma 64 (pp. 45–46). title: 2.19 Ketover shrinkers with Platonic symmetry
text: [ Ketover2016 ] , Theorem 0.1, constructs five families by equivariant Gaussian min-max. The compact doubled solids used in the sweepout describe the genus and symmetry of the construction; compactness of the limiting shrinker is not proved. AE0CC89EB3E2 There are smooth connected embedded self-shrinking surfaces $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ with the following pairs of genus and rotational symmetry group: \[  (g,G)=(3,T_{12}),\quad (5,O_{24}),\quad (7,O_{24}), \quad (11,I_{60}),\quad (19,I_{60}).  \] Here the subscripts give the orders of the tetrahedral, octahedral, and icosahedral rotation groups. The normalization is $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. No explicit parametrization is supplied. The sweepout joins two spherical sheets by one neck for each face of a tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, or icosahedron, respectively. The numbers of necks are $4,6,8,12,20$; the first neck connects the components, so the genus is one less than this number. This is a construction description, not an exact metric model. The min-max limit is multiplicity one. It is complete and proper, has no boundary, and retains the stated genus and symmetry. The construction controls the genus but does not determine compactness, the number of ends, or end asymptotics. In particular, a compact picture suggested by numerical work must not be used to assign zero ends to these proved examples. The proof gives a useful strict Gaussian-area bound: \[  \frac4e < F_{0,1}(\Sigma )=\lambda (\Sigma )<\frac8e.  \] For the doubled cube, the first equivariant width is $4/e$, the second is strictly below twice the first by Lemma 2.4, and the equality of the two widths is excluded in Remark 2.7. Remark 2.5 gives the same construction for the other four symmetry types. These are bounds, not computed entropy values. No uniqueness or stability classification is asserted. The two-parameter equivariant construction alone does not give an index bound for unrestricted variations. Later constructions with similar symmetries need not be different surfaces, and no identification is assumed here. title: 2.20 Sun–Wang–Zhou shrinkers of arbitrarily large entropy

section: 2.20 Sun–Wang–Zhou shrinkers of arbitrarily large entropy
text: The Gaussian-width construction of [ SunWangZhou2024 ] produces shrinkers whose entropy is unbounded, in contrast with the uniform upper bounds for several gluing and low-parameter min-max families. 0177A2718D72 (Sun–Wang–Zhou Gaussian-width shrinkers) For every $2\leq n\leq 6$ there is a sequence of smooth, connected, embedded self-shrinking hypersurfaces $\Sigma _ k^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$. They are normalized by $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, with associated smooth flows $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ k$ for $t<0$. The construction is variational and does not give explicit parametrizations. Each shrinker is complete, proper, boundaryless, and has finite entropy. The construction is a multiplicity-one limit of free-boundary min-max hypersurfaces in exhausting balls with metrics approaching the Gaussian metric. The final shrinker has no free boundary. Write $G_ n=(4\pi )^{-1}e^{-|x|^2/(2n)}g_{\mathrm{Euc}}$ and let $\omega _ k(\mathbb R^{n+1},G_ n)$ be its Gaussian $k$-width, defined by exhaustion. Then \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ k)=\lambda (\Sigma _ k) =\omega _ k(\mathbb R^{n+1},G_ n),\qquad \lambda (\Sigma _ k)\asymp k^{1/(n+1)}.  \] The growth statement means comparison up to positive constants depending on $n$, and in particular $\lambda (\Sigma _ k)\to \infty $. It is not a closed formula for an individual width or a plotted list of computed values. The unbounded entropies ensure infinitely many different examples, without requiring consecutive widths to be strictly different. title: 2.21 Chu–Sun genus-one shrinkers below the shrinking doughnut

section: 2.21 Chu–Sun genus-one shrinkers below the shrinking doughnut
text: The flow construction in [ ChuSun2025 ] gives an embedded genus-one shrinker with strictly less entropy than the Drugan–Nguyen shrinking doughnut. It does not identify the resulting surface with any particular previously constructed example. AE7721D6799F (Chu–Sun lower-entropy genus-one shrinkers) Let $\mathcal T\subset \mathbb R^3$ be the rotationally symmetric compact genus-one shrinker constructed by Drugan–Nguyen (Example 2.9 ). There is a smooth embedded genus-one shrinker $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ satisfying \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma )=\lambda (\Sigma ) <\lambda (\mathcal T)<2.  \] It has dimension two and codimension one, is normalized by $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and yields the smooth self-similar flow $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. The surface is a multiplicity-one tangent-flow model at a genus-one singularity of an ancient level-set flow which is asymptotic, after rescaling as $t\to -\infty $, to $\mathcal T$. The ancient flow is allowed to pass through cylindrical and spherical singularities before the genus-one singularity. Thus the theorem does not assert that this is the first singularity of a smooth ancient flow. The resulting shrinker is complete, proper, and boundaryless. Its compactness, end count, end asymptotics, and symmetry are not determined by this existence statement. No explicit parametrization, exact entropy value, or numerical shape is supplied. Strictly smaller entropy rules out congruence with the chosen shrinking doughnut $\mathcal T$. It does not prove that $\Sigma $ differs from the Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz genus-one example. Remark 1.5 discusses that example and its numerical evidence, without proving the identification. It also does not identify $\mathcal T$ with Angenent's shooting torus. For a shrinker minimizing entropy among all embedded genus-one shrinkers, Theorem 1.4 gives a further alternative: it is noncompact or has Gaussian Morse index exactly $5$. This statement applies to an entropy minimizer, not to every shrinker obtained by the interpolation construction. No uniqueness is asserted. The diagram records the flow construction and strict entropy drop; the final genus-one shrinker is left abstract because its compactness and ends are not specified. title: 3.1 The grim reaper and its cylinders

section: 3.1 The grim reaper and its cylinders
text: 3B1939BC4D74 For unit upward translation, an exact parametrization in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=(x,y,-\log \cos x+t),\qquad |x|<\pi /2,\quad y\in \mathbb R^{n-1},\quad t\in \mathbb R.  \] For $n=1$ omit $y$. More generally the planar curve of speed $c>0$ has height $-c^{-1}\log \cos (cx)+ct$, on $|x|<\pi /(2c)$. The curve and all its Euclidean products are complete, properly embedded, noncompact, and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. Their motion is eternal. At unit speed the curve has curvature magnitude $\cos x$ and total curvature $\pi $. Its two ends have the vertical asymptotes $x=\pm \pi /2$. The product is invariant under translations in its $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ factor. For $n\geq 2$ its second fundamental form has rank one; in $\mathbb R^3$ its Gauss curvature is zero, so it is not strictly convex. As a translating graph it is stable for compactly supported variations of the translator weighted area. This is weighted stability, not a claim about stability for unweighted Euclidean area. The supplied notes [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Example 1.6, PDF page 4, use downward translation; the displayed surface is its reflection in a horizontal plane. Graphical weighted minimality is discussed in [ HIMWGraphical18 ] , Section 2, PDF page 5. 3B1939BC4D74 For unit upward translation, an exact parametrization in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=(x,y,-\log \cos x+t),\qquad |x|<\pi /2,\quad y\in \mathbb R^{n-1},\quad t\in \mathbb R.  \] For $n=1$ omit $y$. title: 3.2 Tilted grim-reaper cylinders
text: 56A3E33A9D04 Let $a\in \mathbb R$ and $A=1+a^2$. An exact unit-speed upward translator in $\mathbb R^3$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=\left(x,y,-A\log \cos (x/\sqrt A)+ay+t\right),\quad |x|<\frac\pi 2\sqrt A,\quad y,t\in \mathbb R.  \] This is a complete, properly embedded noncompact surface diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$. It has zero Gauss curvature and is invariant under translation in the direction $(0,1,a)$. Its horizontal graph domain is a strip of width $\pi \sqrt{1+a^2}$. The case $a=0$ is the ordinary grim-reaper cylinder. The underlying surface is a rotation and dilation of that cylinder. At a fixed width greater than $\pi $, the two signs of $a$ give the two opposite tilts. Translation in a tangent invariant direction does not change the evolving image. Products with Euclidean factors give higher-dimensional translators. Graphical weighted stability holds, as in the preceding example. See [ HIMWGraphical18 ] , equation (1.4), PDF page 3, with exchanged horizontal coordinates and reflected vertical direction. These cylinders must be distinguished from the strictly convex $\Delta $-wings on strips of the same width. 56A3E33A9D04 Let $a\in \mathbb R$ and $A=1+a^2$. title: 3.3 The rotational bowl translator
text: ECF360A3D482 For each $n\geq 2$, the bowl is the entire graph $z=f(r)$, $r=|x|$ in $\mathbb R^ n$, moving by $z\mapsto z+t$. Its radial profile is specified by the regular ODE \[  \frac{f''}{1+(f')^2}+\frac{n-1}{r}f'=1,\qquad f(0)=f'(0)=0,\qquad f''(0)=1/n.  \] This is an ODE characterization, not an elementary closed formula. The bowl is complete, properly embedded, strictly convex, rotationally invariant, and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. For $n\geq 2$ it has one topological end and gives an eternal flow. Up to a vertical additive constant, its height has asymptotic expansion \[  f(r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C+O(r^{-1})\quad (r\to \infty ).  \] A paraboloid is only a leading approximation, not the exact translator. It is unique among entire rotationally invariant translating graphs, up to translation. In $\mathbb R^3$ it is the only complete entire translating graph, up to the natural rigid motions and normalization. In $\mathbb R^3$, Brendle–Choi's theorem characterizes its flow among noncompact, strictly convex, noncollapsed ancient flows, up to scaling and ambient isometries. These are the hypotheses of the cited classification. Graphical weighted stability holds. The stronger dynamical stability theorem of Clutterbuck–Schnürer–Schulze concerns continuous graphical initial data whose height difference from the bowl tends to zero at spatial infinity; the resulting height difference tends uniformly to zero as time tends to infinity. The supplied notes [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4 and Theorem 4.1, PDF pages 10–11, describe the construction and classification. The original ODE and asymptotic analysis is [ CSS07 ] , Section 2, Lemmas 2.1–2.2; its Theorem 1.1 gives the stated dynamical stability. The ancient classification is [ BrendleChoi19 ] , Theorem 1.1, printed page 36 (PDF page 2). The entropy is $\lambda (\mathrm{Bowl}^ n)=\lambda (S^{n-1}(\sqrt{2(n-1)}))$, in particular $\sqrt{2\pi /e}$ in $\mathbb R^3$. This follows from [ SunWang2025 ] , Example 3.6 and Corollary 2.4 with Lemma 2.5, PDF pp. 8–11; it is not an identity for the fixed-center Gaussian area of the bowl. title: 3.4 Rotational translating catenoids
text: 72E3A9DEA98C For every neck radius $R>0$ and $n\geq 2$, there is a rotational translating hypersurface with two ends. These are also called winglike translators. They move upward with unit speed. A convenient numerical description uses meridian arclength $s$ and tangent angle $\alpha $: \[  r'=\cos \alpha ,\qquad z'=\sin \alpha ,\qquad \alpha '=\cos \alpha -\frac{n-1}{r}\sin \alpha , \qquad (r,z,\alpha )(0)=(R,0,\pi /2).  \] Revolution gives $(r(s)\omega ,z(s)+t)$ with $\omega \in S^{n-1}$ and $t\in \mathbb R$. The arclength system is obtained from $\vec H=e_{n+1}^{\perp }$ and is not a closed formula. The surface is complete, embedded, noncompact and nonconvex, with topology $S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$. In $\mathbb R^3$ it is an annulus, not an entire graph. Outside the neck the two ends are radial graphs. Each has expansion \[  f_\pm (r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C_\pm +O(r^{-1}).  \] In particular the two ends go to spatial infinity and the complete surface is proper. The parameter controls the neck radius. The supplied survey describes the limiting double bowl with a singular point on the axis as the neck parameter tends to zero. See [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4, PDF page 10. The original construction and end expansion are [ CSS07 ] , Lemma 2.3, PDF pages 5–7 of the author preprint. title: 3.5 Strictly convex delta-wing translators
text: B72E7DC6B42E For every $b>\pi /2$, there is a complete strictly convex unit-speed translator that is a graph $z=u_ b(x,y)$ over \[  (x,y)\in \mathbb R\times (-b,b),\qquad \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{(u_ b)_ i(u_ b)_ j}{1+|Du_ b|^2}\right)(u_ b)_{ij}=1.  \] This is a nonlinear PDE characterization; no explicit height formula is supplied. The graph is embedded, noncompact, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$, and has positive Gauss curvature everywhere. After centering and a vertical translation, $u_ b(0,0)=0$ is its minimum and $u_ b$ is even in both coordinates. The width is exactly $2b>\pi $. Among complete translators on this strip that are not tilted grim reapers, it is unique up to translation. The centered solution depends smoothly on compact sets under limits of the width parameter. Along the two unbounded horizontal directions, translated graphs converge smoothly to the two oppositely tilted grim-reaper cylinders of the same strip width. Their angle is determined by \[  \cos \theta =\frac{\pi }{2b}.  \] This relation follows from the explicit tilted-cylinder width; the supplied preprint has an inverted ratio in its printed statement of Theorem 2.4. Graphical weighted stability holds. This is a strictly convex surface, whereas the tilted grim-reaper cylinders on the same strip have zero Gauss curvature. See [ HIMWGraphical18 ] , Theorems 1.1, 2.4, 4.1 and 5.7 and Corollary 5.5 (PDF pages 4, 6, 10–12). The construction, uniqueness, and asymptotic results are cited rather than reproduced here. The illustration numerically approximates the rectangular Dirichlet construction in Sections 3–4 at $b=\pi /\sqrt{2}$, then recenters at the minimum and displays a compact height-truncated patch. The paper uses downward translation; the picture reflects the vertical coordinate to match the upward convention here. Profile views compare the computed surface with the exact limiting profile $-2\log \cos (y/\sqrt{2})$ and longitudinal limiting slopes $\pm 1$. The computation has finite-domain and discretization error; it is not an explicit formula or a certified numerical enclosure. title: 3.14 Nonrotational entire convex translators
text: 0F00F9295CD9 In every dimension $n\geq 3$, Xu-Jia Wang constructs entire convex solutions $u:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ of the unit-speed upward translator equation \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}\right)u_{ij}=1  \] whose level sets are not spheres or round cylinders in any orthogonal coordinate system. This is an existence construction, not an explicit formula. The graphs are embedded, complete, proper and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$; the last three facts also follow directly from being smooth entire graphs. Their flows exist for all $t\in \mathbb R$ by translation. They are convex and break the spherical or cylindrical rotational pattern of the bowl and its Euclidean products. The corresponding statement for complete entire graphs in $\mathbb R^3$ is false: there the bowl is the only example. Under spatial blow-down $u_ h(x)=h^{-1}u(\sqrt h\, x)$, Wang's theorem gives, after rotations depending on $h$, a quadratic limit of the form \[  \frac{x_1^2+\cdots +x_ k^2}{2(k-1)},\qquad 2\leq k\leq n.  \] The theorem does not rule out slow rotation of the axes as $h\to \infty $. This is an asymptotic limit, not a formula for $u$. The same paper also constructs nonrotational complete convex graphical translators over slab regions. No uniqueness theorem for the general higher-dimensional families is claimed here. For the construction in Section 5, write $x'=(x_1,\ldots ,x_{n-1})$. Wang solves a convex Dirichlet problem on ellipsoids in the Legendre-dual variables, fixes an unequal ratio of the dual level-set widths, and passes to a limit after transforming back. When $n\geq 3$, the choice $\theta >1$ in (5.8) gives an entire solution. This construction retains rotations in $x'$ and reflection in $x_ n$. Wang's term $k$-rotational also requires independence of the other coordinates: partial rotation symmetry alone does not make these examples bowls or bowl products. For $n=3$, the graph lies in $\mathbb R^4$, with $x_4=u(x_1,x_2,x_3)$. A horizontal level $\{ u=h\} $ can be drawn in the base $\mathbb R^3$; the construction has bounded sublevel sets by (5.13). The figure uses a convex schematic for these levels and also offers the graph slice $x_2=0$. The figure uses a convex schematic for these levels and also offers the graph slice $x_2=0$. title: 3.6 Translators with prescribed apex curvatures
text: D68656E88625 Let $k_1,\ldots ,k_ n\geq 0$ with $\sum _ i k_ i=1$. Hoffman–Ilmanen–Martín–White construct a complete properly embedded translating graph over an open domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$. After reflecting their downward convention to upward translation, it satisfies \[  \min u=u(0)=0,\qquad D^2u(0)=\operatorname {diag}(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n).  \] These equations specify apex data, not an explicit global formula. The function is even in every coordinate. If $k_ i=0$ it is invariant under translation in the $i$-th coordinate; if $k_ i>0$, then $D_ i u$ has the same sign as $x_ i$ away from $x_ i=0$. Equal apex curvatures $k_ i=k_ j$ give invariance under rotations in the $(x_ i,x_ j)$-plane. The domain is either all of $\mathbb R^ n$ or a slab $\{ |x_ i|<b\} $. In the slab case the corresponding $k_ i$ is strictly larger than every other $k_ j$. If the two largest prescribed curvatures are equal, the resulting graph is entire. The supplied edition obtains an $(n-2)$-parameter family of pairwise noncongruent entire examples this way. The construction gives existence and the listed symmetries, but does not assert general uniqueness or convexity of every higher-dimensional graph. In particular, apex positivity alone is not a global convexity theorem. See [ HIMWGraphical18 ] , Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 8.2, PDF page 18. The source also has a prescribed-width slab construction in Section 11; its final discussion explicitly leaves general convexity open. For $n=2$, the figure compares three surface cases in $\mathbb R^3$: $(k_1,k_2)=(0,1)$ gives the grim-reaper cylinder $u(x,y)=-\log \cos y$ on $\mathbb R\times (-\pi /2,\pi /2)$, while $(1/2,1/2)$ gives the rotational bowl. The intermediate picture reuses a numerical $\Delta $-wing on the strip $\mathbb R\times (-\pi /\sqrt2,\pi /\sqrt2)$, obtained by the rectangular Dirichlet construction in Sections 3–4; its measured apex Hessian is approximately $(0.2443,0.7557)$, not an exact prescribed pair. The bowl profile is integrated numerically. All three translate by $t e_3$ for $t\in \mathbb R$. The principal-section view compares the graph with the local Taylor data $\frac12 k_ i s^2$; those parabolas are not global translator formulas. title: 3.7 Scherkenoid translators
text: C6C5A44F27CC Hoffman–Martín–White construct Scherkenoids for $0<\alpha <\pi $ and $w\geq \pi $ as complete, properly embedded, singly periodic translator surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$; see [ HMW20 ] , Theorems 2.3 and 9.2. In the catalogue's upward convention, the fundamental piece is the graph of $U$ over \[  \Omega (\alpha ,w)=\{ (x,y):0<y<w,\  x>y\cot \alpha \} ,  \] with $U\to +\infty $ on the two horizontal rays and $U\to -\infty $ on the finite slanted edge. The graph closes along the two vertical lines above the corners. Repeated half-turns about those lines produce the complete surface, with period $2(w\cot \alpha ,w,0)$. This is a boundary-value construction, not a closed formula for $U$. The connected illustration fixes $\alpha =\pi /2$ and allows $w$ to vary. It shows how a single central sheet opens into alternating wings. Far along a wing, after recentering height, the limiting graph has the explicit profile \[  G_ w(x,y)=-\left(\frac{w}{\pi }\right)^2\log \sin \left(\frac{\pi y}{w}\right) +x\sqrt{\left(\frac{w}{\pi }\right)^2-1},\qquad x\in \mathbb R,\quad 0<y<w.  \] This formula describes the tilted grim-reaper limit, not the whole Scherkenoid. For $w=\pi $ the tilt vanishes. In the upward convention, the height limits are the plane $x=y\cot \alpha $ as $z\to -\infty $ and the planes $y=nw$, $n\in \mathbb Z$, as $z\to +\infty $. The drawing follows Figures 5 and 11 and Section 9 of [ HMW20 ] , arXiv version 4, pages 7 and 26–30. Its joining profile is schematic, not a numerical solution of the translator equation. The paper uses downward velocity; reflecting height gives the upward flow $M_ t=M+t e_3$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. See also the earlier survey [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 5. No stability or entropy conclusion is inferred from the drawing. title: 3.8 The pitchfork translator
text: B5E7AB44607B The pitchfork is a complete, properly embedded, simply connected, nongraphical translator in $\mathbb R^3$. The supplied notes describe it as a limit of Scherk-type examples, without an explicit formula. It has genus zero. This distinguishes it from Nguyen's periodic infinite-genus tridents despite their similar asymptotic plane arrangements. After reflection to upward translation, it is asymptotic to one plane as $z\to -\infty $ and to three parallel planes as $z\to +\infty $. These are height-direction asymptotics, not a claim that the surface has four topological ends. Its translation yields an eternal noncompact flow. The later construction paper records finite topology and quadratic area growth for its pitchfork subfamily. See [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 5 and Figure 7, PDF pages 11–12, and [ HMW20 ] . The existence proof is external. The full construction supplies a pitchfork for each half-width $w\geq \pi $, lying in $|y|<w$. Theorem 1 of [ MSTW26 ] proves uniqueness up to isometry for fixed width in this semigraphical family. Moreover, [ GMM25 ] , Theorem 1.5, characterizes pitchforks among complete embedded simply connected translators of finite width, entropy $3$, and containing a vertical line. These hypotheses are essential to the stated classification. To read the picture, remove the vertical $z$-axis. One component is a graph $z=v(x,y)$ over $\mathbb R\times (0,w)$; the other is its image under $(x,y,z)\mapsto (-x,-y,z)$. In the upward convention the boundary values are \[  v(x,0)=-\infty \quad (x<0),\qquad v(x,0)=+\infty \quad (x>0),\qquad v(x,w)=+\infty .  \] Theorem 12.1 and Corollary 12.2 of [ HMW20 ] give the smooth extension along the axis, negative Gauss curvature, and the planar and tilted-grim-reaper asymptotics. For $w=\pi $, the grim-reaper profile, after vertical recentering at $y=\pi /2$, is $-\log \sin y$ for $0<y<\pi $. This is an asymptotic profile, not a formula for the pitchfork. The interactive drawing illustrates this width using two colored halves and horizontal sections, following Figures 6 and 14 of that paper. Its connecting geometry is schematic, not a computed solution of the translator equation. title: 3.9 Nguyen translating tridents
text: 27C982677562 Nguyen's tridents are complete periodic embedded translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ obtained by desingularizing a grim-reaper cylinder and a plane. We use unit upward velocity $e_3$, so $M_ t=M_0+t e_3$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. There is no explicit global formula for the completed translator. They are noncompact and have infinite genus. A repeating row of Scherk saddle connections resolves the intersection; the intersecting input surfaces are not themselves a trident. In the upward convention there is one asymptotic plane as $z\to -\infty $ and three parallel asymptotic planes as $z\to +\infty $. These describe height-direction asymptotics, not a count of topological ends of the full periodic surface. Nguyen's construction applies at sufficiently small positive scales. The later semigraphical construction agrees with these examples in that range; its tridents are properly embedded and have entropy $3$ [ HMWTridents22 ] , Theorem 1 and pp. 2–3. This entropy is not identified with centered Gaussian area. The local minimal ingredient is $\sin v=\sinh u\sinh w$, with $(u,v,w)\in \mathbb R^3$ and period $2\pi $ in $v$. Its four wings are attached to two planar wings and two grim-reaper wings. In the unit upward convention the limiting inputs are $z=-\log \cos y$, $|y|<\pi /2$, $x\in \mathbb R$, and the plane $y=0$. See [ Nguyen09 ] , Theorem 1, Sections 1.2–1.4 and Section 2 (Definitions 4–5), and [ HMWTridents22 ] , Figures 1–2. The latter figures use downward translation; here height is reflected. The interactive picture is an original smooth deformation of the Scherk ingredient, with three periods shown. Its half-surface view exposes the saddle connections. Its neck scale is a drawing parameter: the unbalancing, cutoff matching, and final nonlinear correction in Nguyen's proof have not been computed. In particular, its fixed illustrative half-width $\pi /2$ is the limiting input width, not the width of a finite-period trident. title: 3.10 Finite-genus translators with three ends
text: 85D3C19BE7E6 Dávila–del Pino–Nguyen construct complete embedded orientable translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ with finite topology and large genus. The construction desingularizes an intersecting bowl translator and translating catenoid. It is a gluing construction, not an explicit formula. The examples have three asymptotically paraboloidal ends. They are noncompact; their translation gives an eternal flow. The high-genus connecting region replaces a circle of intersection of the model surfaces by a Scherk-like arrangement of small tunnels. The genus restriction is part of the construction: this statement does not supply examples of every prescribed small genus or a uniqueness theorem. The supplied notes [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4, PDF page 11, describe the gluing configuration and the large-genus restriction. The original paper [ DPN17 ] , Theorem 1.1, Figure 2, and Section 2, supplies the construction. The illustration separates the numerically integrated bowl–catenoid input from a connected schematic of the tunnel belt. The latter is not a numerical solution of the translator equation. Its period counts are illustrative, and no unproved stability or entropy value is assigned. 85D3C19BE7E6 Dávila–del Pino–Nguyen construct complete embedded orientable translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ with finite topology and large genus. title: 3.15 Translators with an Angenent-torus end
text:
BF18BDD64F8E Let $S_ A\subset \mathbb R^3$ be an embedded Angenent self-shrinking torus, normalized by $\vec H_{S_ A}=-X^\perp /2$. Sun–Wang construct complete embedded three-dimensional translators $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^4=\mathbb R^3_ x	imes \mathbb R_ z$ satisfying \[  \vec H_\Sigma =e_4^\perp ,\qquad M_ t=\Sigma +t e_4,\qquad -\infty <t<\infty .  \] These are variationally constructed hypersurfaces, not explicit parametrized solutions. At sufficiently large height each has the exact graph representation \[  \Sigma \cap \{ z\geq z_0\}  =\left\{ \left(\sqrt z\, [x+u(x,z)
u _ A(x)],zight): x\in S_ A,\  z\geq z_0ight\} ,\qquad \| u(\cdot ,z)\| _{C^0(S_ A)}=O(z^{-\epsilon })  \] for some $\epsilon >0$. The unknown function $u$ is solved for by the construction. In particular, the auxiliary expression obtained by setting $u=0$ is not asserted to be a translator. The translators have codimension one and are smooth, noncompact, complete, and properly embedded. Sun–Wang's general construction can have a singular set of dimension at most $n-7$ for an $n$-dimensional translator in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$; for the present $n=3$ this set is empty. There is a compact core and one end diffeomorphic to $S_ A	imes [z_0,\infty )$. Thus a fixed time slice has one topological end, and its sufficiently high horizontal cross-sections have genus one. The translator is a three-manifold: a surface genus is not assigned to it, and the theorem does not identify its compact core as a solid torus. Its unique tangent flow at backward infinity is the multiplicity-one shrinking cylinder generated by $S_ A	imes \mathbb R$. Equivalently, \[  R^{-1/2}(\Sigma -R e_4)\longrightarrow S_ A	imes \mathbb R \quad \hbox{as }R\longrightarrow \infty .  \] This parabolic blow-down cylinder and the single topological end are different notions. Write $I_ A=\operatorname {ind}_{F}(S_ A)$ for the number of negative eigenvalues of \[  -L_{S_ A},\qquad L_{S_ A}=\Delta _{S_ A}-	frac 12 X^	op \! \cdot 
abla _{S_ A} +|A_{S_ A}|^2+	frac 12,  \] counted with multiplicity. The translating ends have an $I_ A$-parameter construction, indexed by a ball in $\mathbb R^{I_ A}$ for each sufficiently large cutoff. No exact numerical value of $I_ A$ is needed here. These parameters include ambient translations; they are not a count of parameters after quotienting by rigid motions. The completions need not form a smooth or single-valued family across a fattening parameter. A rotationally invariant subfamily can be chosen. The chosen completions minimize Ilmanen's weighted area $\mathcal I=\int e^ z\, d\mathcal H^3$ locally with their boundary fixed. Consequently they are stable for compactly supported variations of that weighted functional. This statement is not a claim of entropy stability or dynamical stability under mean curvature flow. Their entropy is finite and satisfies the exact identity \[  \lambda (\Sigma )=F(S_ A	imes \mathbb R)=F(S_ A)=\lambda (S_ A) = rac1{4\pi }\int _{S_ A}e^{-|x|^2/4}\, d\mathcal H^2.  \] No closed numerical value or value of $F_{0,1}(\Sigma )$ is supplied by this construction. Nonuniqueness occurs within this same family. There is a rotationally invariant translating end $\Sigma _ e$ for which the associated closed set $T[\Sigma _ e]$ has nonempty interior and \[  \partial T[\Sigma _ e]=T^+\sqcup T^-.  \] The two distinct boundary hypersurfaces are complete smooth embedded $\mathcal I$-minimizing translators, exponentially asymptotic to the same $\Sigma _ e$. Their normalized graph difference decays exponentially in height. This is nonuniqueness of minimizing completions of a fixed end; it is not an assertion that there are exactly two arbitrary translators with that end. For the fixed ball of ends supplied by the construction, the parameters at which fattening occurs form a meager subset. Off that subset there is a unique $\mathcal I$-minimizing completion exponentially asymptotic to the specified end. The uniqueness statement is restricted to this minimizing class and this asymptotic condition. The original torus is constructed in [ Angenent1992 ] , unnumbered theorem on PDF page 1 of the supplied preprint; its original normalization is converted by multiplying the reference immersion by $\sqrt2$. The translator construction is [ SunWang2025 ] , Theorems 1.1 and 3.7 (PDF pages 2 and 12), Theorem 4.1 (page 28), and Theorem 4.3 (pages 32–34). The compact-core and single-end statement follows from Lemma 2.5 and the graphical end description in Lemma 3.2 (pages 9–10). The entropy identity is Corollary 2.4 and Lemma 2.5 (pages 8–9). Fattening and its genericity are Theorem 5.1 (page 35, proved on pages 38–39) and Corollary 4.5 (page 34). The construction is not an exhaustive classification, and its realization as a type-II blow-up of a closed flow is stated as Conjecture 4.6 in that paper. title: 3.16 Translators with high-genus spherical-doubling ends
text: 9B1B88A4317F Fix an integer $m$ sufficiently large. In the spherical-doubling construction of Kapouleas–McGrath, choose two latitude circles and $m$ aligned bridge sites on each circle. Their theorem gives a smooth closed embedded shrinker $S_ m\subset \mathbb R^3$, obtained by connecting two nearby copies of the radius-two sphere with $2m$ small catenoidal bridges. Its genus is $2m-1$. This specifies a concrete subfamily of their construction; there is no effective lower threshold for $m$ or explicit formula for $S_ m$ in this statement. Applying the Sun–Wang construction to $S_ m$ produces complete embedded translators $\Sigma _ m^3\subset \mathbb R^4$ with \[  \vec H_{\Sigma _ m}=e_4^\perp ,\qquad M_ t=\Sigma _ m+t e_4,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] and, outside a compact set, \[  \Sigma _ m= \left\{ \left(\sqrt z\, [x+u_ m(x,z)\nu _{S_ m}(x)],z\right): x\in S_ m,\  z\geq z_0\right\} ,\qquad \| u_ m(\cdot ,z)\| _{C^0(S_ m)}=O(z^{-\epsilon _ m})  \] for some $\epsilon _ m>0$. Both the shrinker and the translator are existence constructions; the displayed formula contains an unknown correction and is not an explicit solution. Each translator is a smooth, complete, properly embedded, noncompact hypersurface, with one end diffeomorphic to $S_ m\times [z_0,\infty )$. The genus $2m-1$ belongs to the two-dimensional horizontal cross-section. No surface genus or complete three-manifold topology is assigned to $\Sigma _ m$. The unique tangent flow at backward infinity is generated by $S_ m\times \mathbb R$ with multiplicity one. Thus these examples have a different prescribed shrinker from the Angenent-torus-end examples, the bowl, and the previously catalogued three-ended translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$. For each fixed $S_ m$ the end construction has $I_ m=\operatorname {ind}_ F(S_ m)$ parameters before quotienting by ambient translations. The exact index is not computed by the cited construction. One may choose an end and a minimizing completion invariant under the finite symmetry group $\mathcal G_ m=D_{2m}\times \mathbb Z_2$ of order $4m$, where $D_{2m}$ here denotes the dihedral group of order $2m$. Symmetry is asserted for such selected examples, not for every member of the full $I_ m$-parameter family. The completions are locally $\mathcal I$-minimizing for $\mathcal I=\int e^ z\, d\mathcal H^3$, hence stable for compactly supported variations of that functional. The generic uniqueness result concerns minimizing completions exponentially asymptotic to a fixed constructed end. No specific fattening example for these $S_ m$ is proved in the cited sources. The entropy is exactly the Gaussian area of the prescribed shrinker: \[  \lambda (\Sigma _ m)=F(S_ m)=\lambda (S_ m)<2F(S^2(2))=\frac8e.  \] The strict upper bound follows by applying the area inequality of Kapouleas–McGrath in the Gaussian metric $g=e^{-|x|^2/4}g_{\rm Euc}$ and dividing its surface area by $4\pi $. It is a consequence of the two cited theorems, not a numerical approximation. No individual numerical entropy or value of $F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ m)$ is recorded. title: 3.11 Doubly periodic Scherk translators
text: D24DEEE97A5F For every $0<\alpha <\pi $ and $0<w<\pi $, Hoffman–Martín–White construct a complete properly embedded translator in $\mathbb R^3$. In their downward convention, a fundamental piece is a graph over the parallelogram of height $w$, angle $\alpha $, and a uniquely selected base length $L(\alpha ,w)>0$, with boundary values $-\infty $ on the horizontal sides and $+\infty $ on the other sides. Half-turns about its four vertical boundary lines extend it to the complete doubly periodic surface. Reflecting $z$ gives our upward normalization $\mathbf H=e_3^\perp $ and the eternal flow $M_ t=M+te_3$, $t\in \mathbb R$. This is an elliptic boundary-value construction, not Scherk's explicit minimal-surface formula. The surface has infinite genus and strictly negative Gauss curvature. Its infinitely many asymptotic parallel planes force infinite entropy. The topological end count and centered Gaussian area are not evaluated here. Uniqueness up to ambient isometry holds for the specified angle and width. Stability of a graphical fundamental piece does not establish stability of the full reflected surface. The illustration uses the rectangular case $\alpha =w=\pi /2$ in Figures 3 and 8 of the source. In the upward convention, the centred fundamental graph $z=v(x,y)$ satisfies \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{v_ i v_ j}{1+|Dv|^2}\right)v_{ij}=1, \qquad (x,y)\in (-L/2,L/2)\times (-w/2,w/2),  \] with $v\to +\infty $ on $y=\pm w/2$ and $v\to -\infty $ on $x=\pm L/2$. The base length is selected by the boundary-value problem, not an independent parameter; Theorem 5.1 gives $L>w$ in this rectangular case. The picture follows the finite-boundary construction in the proof of Theorem 3.1: replace the infinite data by $\pm 2.5$, impose $v(0,0)=0$, and solve numerically for both $v$ and $L$. A $257\times 257$ grid gives $L\approx 2.4483$ for this truncated problem. This number is not a certified value of the infinite-boundary length. Only $|z|\le 1.5$ is displayed. The small unresolved regions at the four vertical corner lines are filled by interpolation; the remaining surface comes from the numerical graph. The periodic view repeats the patch by vertical half-turns, preserving height, and shows finitely many copies of the resulting infinite arrangement. In centred coordinates these graph domains occupy alternating rectangles, with horizontal periods $(2L,0,0)$ and $(0,2w,0)$. The height slider changes only the displayed truncation. Neither mesh refinement nor the small discrete residual supplies a certified error bound for the complete translator. Sources: [ HMW20 ] , Theorems 2.3, 3.1, 5.1 and 6.1, Figures 3 and 8–10, and the discussion on pp. 9 and 17; [ MSTW26 ] , Theorem 1. title: 3.12 Helicoid-like translators
text: E6CC94303132 For each $0<w<\pi $, there is a complete properly embedded helicoid-like translator in $\mathbb R^3$. In the downward convention, its fundamental graph over $\mathbb R\times (0,w)$ has alternating infinite boundary values, switching at $(0,0)$ and $(\widehat x,w)$, where $\widehat x>0$ is selected by the solution. Half-turn reflection about the two vertical boundary lines gives horizontal period $2(\widehat x,w,0)$. Reflection in a horizontal plane converts it to $M_ t=M+te_3$, $t\in \mathbb R$. It is noncompact and has strictly negative Gauss curvature. Successive simply connected strip pieces join along a line in a chain, giving a plane topologically, with genus zero and one topological end. This is a topological deduction from the strip decomposition. Its asymptotic family of parallel vertical planes implies $\lambda (M)=+\infty $. No centered Gaussian-area value is recorded. The axis is oblique to these planes; an ordinary minimal helicoid is not this translator. Sources: [ HMW20 ] , Theorems 2.3 and 11.1 and Remark 11.2; [ MSTW26 ] , Theorem 1 and Section 4, proves uniqueness up to isometry for fixed fundamental width. The earlier paper's open uniqueness question is therefore superseded. The picture shows only the semigraphical arrangement, not a numerical PDE solution. title: 3.13 Annuloid translators in slabs
text: 4887FC9B88DC For every inner half-width $b\geq \pi /2$ and necksize $s>0$, Hoffman–Martín–White construct a complete properly embedded annular translator in $\mathbb R^3$. Their necksize is the distance from the $z$-axis to $M\cap \{ y=0\} $; it is not assumed to be a circular neck radius. The surface lies in a slab $|y|\leq B$, has both vertical coordinate-plane reflection symmetries, and is nonrotational. Its topology is $S^1\times \mathbb R$: genus zero and two ends. After reflecting the source's downward translator, $M_ t=M+te_3$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. The positive-height asymptotics are four planes $y=\pm b,\pm B$, counted with multiplicity if $b=B$; the negative-height end of the ambient space sees no surface. Four asymptotic planes in one height direction do not mean four topological ends. The outer half-width $B$ is an output of the construction, not an independent prescribed parameter. Capped and uncapped behaviors occur. No closed formula or uniqueness for fixed $(b,s)$ is supplied. The entropy is exactly $4$, by [ HMWAnnuli24 ] , Remark 7.9, using [ GMM25 ] , Corollary 8.5. This is not a fixed-center Gaussian-area identity. Existence and the parameters are in Theorem 1.1, Definition 1.2, and Sections 7 and 22 of [ HMWAnnuli24 ] . title: 4.1 Expanding smoothings of planar corners
text: The convention throughout these entries is $\vec H=X^\perp /2$ for the time-one profile. Thus $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M$, $t>0$, is the corresponding flow. The positive weight for variational statements is $e^{|X|^2/4}$; minimizing this weighted area locally will be called $E$-minimizing. 72808FA576A9 (Even graphical corner expanders) For every $\kappa >0$ there is a smooth even function $\phi _\kappa :\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ satisfying \[  \frac{\phi _\kappa ''}{1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2} +\frac{x\phi _\kappa '-\phi _\kappa }{2}=0, \qquad \phi _\kappa '(0)=0, \qquad \lim _{|x|\to \infty }\frac{\phi _\kappa (x)}{|x|}=\kappa .  \] The profile $\Gamma _\kappa =\{ (x,\phi _\kappa (x)):x\in \mathbb R\} $ is a smooth complete properly embedded noncompact curve in $\mathbb R^2$, with topology $\mathbb R$, reflection symmetry, and two ends asymptotic to the rays of $y=\kappa |x|$. It is $E$-minimizing against compact replacements. Its curvature vector is nonzero and points along the upward graph normal: writing $q=\phi _\kappa -x\phi _\kappa '$ gives $q'=-x(1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2)q/2$ and $\phi _\kappa ''=(1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2)q/2$, with $q(0)>0$. The source gives the quantitative estimate, for $x>0$, \[  0\leq \phi _\kappa (x)-\kappa x \leq \min \left\{ \frac{2e(\kappa +2)}{x}e^{-x^2/4},\, 3\kappa +2\right\} .  \] The flow $\sqrt t\, \Gamma _\kappa $, $t\in (0,\infty )$, smooths the corner at time zero. These are ODE-defined profiles, not elementary closed formulas. Source: [ Ding20 ] , Section 4, equations (4.9)–(4.15), printed pp. 373–374, supplied PDF pp. 15–16. The figure shows a numerical ODE profile with $\phi (0)=1$. text: D3CC5E948716 (Entire radial cone smoothings) For $n\geq 2$ and $\kappa >0$, consider \[  M_\kappa =\{ (x,\phi _\kappa (|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} \subset \mathbb R^{n+1},  \] where $\phi _\kappa $ is the smooth radial solution constructed with \[  \frac{\phi _\kappa ''}{1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2} +\frac{n-1}{r}\phi _\kappa ' +\frac{r\phi _\kappa '-\phi _\kappa }{2}=0, \qquad \phi _\kappa '(0)=0, \qquad \lim _{r\to \infty }\frac{\phi _\kappa (r)}r=\kappa .  \] The equation at $r=0$ is interpreted by smooth radial extension; it implies $\phi _\kappa ''(0)=\phi _\kappa (0)/(2n)$. This is an ODE construction, not a closed formula. The hypersurface is smooth, complete, properly embedded, noncompact, rotationally symmetric, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$, and $E$-minimizing against compact replacements. It has one conical end and nondecreasing height. The estimate \[  0\leq \phi _\kappa (r)-\kappa r \leq ((n+1)\kappa +2)\min \{ 1,r^{-1}\} ,\qquad r>0,  \] records the rate at which it approaches its cone. Its flow is $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M_\kappa $ for $t>0$, with initial cone $z=\kappa |x|$. Source: [ Ding20 ] , Section 4, equations (4.1), (4.7), and (4.8), printed pp. 371–373, supplied PDF pp. 13–15. section: 4.4 Two-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones
text: 4F35D93CA4BD (Disconnected double-cone smoothings) Let $n\geq 2$, write $(x,z)\in \mathbb R^ n\times \mathbb R$, and let \[  D_\alpha =\{ (x,z):|x|=|z|\tan \alpha \} ,\qquad 0<\alpha <\pi /2.  \] With $\phi _{\cot \alpha }$ from Example 4.3 , the two-sheeted expander is \[  M_\alpha ^{(2)} =\{ (x,\phi _{\cot \alpha }(|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\}  \mathbin {\cup } \{ (x,-\phi _{\cot \alpha }(|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} .  \] This display specifies the surface using ODE-defined functions. Its two components are smooth, complete, properly embedded convex entire graphs, each diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. The union is noncompact, invariant under rotations about the $z$-axis and under $z\mapsto -z$, and has two oppositely directed conical ends. The flow $\sqrt t\, M_\alpha ^{(2)}$, $t>0$, approaches $D_\alpha $ as $t\downarrow 0$. Existence and uniqueness of each rotational single-lobe graphical profile are established in [ AIC95 ] , Lemma 2(i), printed p. 1947, supplied PDF p. 12. Theorem 4, printed pp. 1950–1951, PDF pp. 15–16, provides a critical angle $\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)\in (0,\pi /2)$. For $\alpha <\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)$ the level-set flow of the double cone is exactly the two-sheeted flow. For angles above this threshold there are also connected smoothings, so the graphical uniqueness statement does not assert uniqueness among all flows from the cone. The critical-angle decimal estimates later in that paper are numerical. section: 4.5 One-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones
text: 3A4775A9BD2C (Connected double-cone smoothings) For $n\geq 2$ and a neck parameter $a>0$, the initial value problem \[  u''=(1+(u')^2)\left(\frac{n-1}{u}+\frac{u-zu'}2\right), \qquad u(0)=a,\quad u'(0)=0,  \] defines a positive, smooth, even profile on $\mathbb R$. Rotating it gives \[  M_ a=\{ (u(z)\omega ,z):z\in \mathbb R,\  \omega \in S^{n-1}\}  \subset \mathbb R^{n+1}.  \] This is a smooth complete properly embedded noncompact expander with topology $S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$, rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, and two conical ends. The profile is increasing for $z>0$. Its limiting aperture depends on $a$; the formula is an ODE specification, not an elementary expression. The evolution is $\sqrt t\, M_ a$ for $t>0$. For every $\alpha >\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)$ there exists such a connected expander asymptotic to $D_\alpha $ from Example 4.4 . It gives a second thin evolution from that cone alongside the disconnected two-sheeted solution. The cited theorem uses a strict inequality and does not establish a universal uniqueness assertion for the one-sheeted profile. Source: [ AIC95 ] , Lemma 2(ii), Lemma 3, and Theorem 4, printed pp. 1947–1951, supplied PDF pp. 12–16. These qualitative expander statements are proved in the source; its separate computed higher-genus shrinker and numerical threshold estimates are not needed here. title: 4.6 One-sided expanders from mean-convex cones
text: A6044506F79A (Ding's smooth minimizing expanders) Let $C\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be an $n$-dimensional $C^{3,\beta }$-regular cone, $0<\beta <1$, regular away from its vertex, with a $C^{3,\beta }$ embedded link in $S^ n$. Assume that $C$ is mean convex but not area minimizing, that $\partial \Omega =C$, and that its mean curvature vector points into the chosen domain $\Omega $ wherever it is nonzero. Then there is a unique smooth complete embedded $E$-minimizing self-expanding hypersurface $M\subset \Omega $ with tangent cone $C$ at infinity. Its mean curvature vector is everywhere nonzero and points into $\Omega $, and \[  \{ \sqrt t\, M:t>0\}   \] is a foliation of $\Omega $ moving by mean curvature flow. The normalization is $\vec H=X^\perp /2$. This is an existence theorem for a family determined by the cone and the chosen side, not an explicit parametrization. The uniqueness just stated includes the chosen-side and minimizing hypotheses. Its topology, symmetry, and number of ends depend on the chosen cone. Source: [ Ding20 ] , Theorem 1.1, printed p. 361, supplied PDF p. 3, and Theorem 6.12, printed pp. 402–403, PDF pp. 44–45. The broader minimizing-current existence theorem in that paper can have singularities and is not being substituted for this smooth theorem. The figure is a schematic of the cone, selected domain, and expanding leaves. title: 4.2 Self-expanding planar tree networks
text: 16898F334139 (Regular expanding trees with prescribed rays) A regular planar network consists of smooth branches meeting only at triple junctions, with angles $120$ degrees at every junction. A self-expanding network $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^2$ satisfies \[  \vec k=\frac{X^\perp }{2}  \] on each open branch; its time evolution is $\Sigma _ t=\sqrt t\, \Sigma $, $t>0$, with the same angle condition. It is a network flow and is not a smooth immersed curve at its junctions. For finitely many distinct prescribed rays from the origin, connected tree-like expanders provide smoothings in this network sense. Existence for three rays, including uniqueness of the tree, and existence for more rays are recalled in [ INS19 ] , Section 7, printed p. 70, supplied PDF p. 32, with attribution there to Schnürer–Schulze and Mazzeo–Sáez respectively. The branches can be described as geodesics for the conformal metric \[  g=e^{|X|^2/2}(dX_1^2+dX_2^2),  \] with the junction balance condition. Noncompact ends approach their assigned rays with Gaussian decay. Two regular expanders with the same asymptotic rays coincide if they are in the same topological class: the comparison deformation must retain distinct junctions and the prescribed asymptotic ends, as in the source definition. This does not assert uniqueness across different network topologies. See [ INS19 ] , Lemmas 4.1 and 4.3 and Theorem 4.4, printed pp. 49–51, supplied PDF pp. 11–13. The source uses $\vec k=\psi ^\perp $ and $\sqrt{2t}\, \psi $; our profile is $\Sigma =\sqrt2\, \psi $. Nontrivial networks arise from a geodesic boundary-value construction. The exact balanced special case \[  \bigcup _{j=0}^2\{ r(\cos (2\pi j/3),\sin (2\pi j/3)):r\geq 0\}   \] is the stationary $Y$ network. It illustrates the junction condition. The accompanying picture instead computes a nonstationary four-ended example, using the geodesic construction of [ MS07 ] , Sections 2–3. In Euclidean arclength $s$, write the tangent as $(\cos \theta ,\sin \theta )$. Then \[  x'=\cos \theta ,\qquad y'=\sin \theta ,\qquad \theta '=\frac{-x\sin \theta +y\cos \theta }{2}.  \] Shoot the upper-right branch from $(x,y,\theta )=(a,0,\pi /3)$ toward the ray of angle $\pi /4$. Numerically, $a\approx 0.385405$ in our normalization. Reflections in the coordinate axes and the straight segment $[-a,a]\times \{ 0\} $ give the displayed tree, with triple junctions at $(\pm a,0)$ and asymptotic rays at angles $\pi /4+j\pi /2$, $j=0,1,2,3$. A quarter-turn gives the second tree. The two pictures are congruent by rotation but have different connections when the four asymptotic ends are held fixed. Both have four ends and no cycles. These are numerical ODE approximations, not closed formulas or a classification of all network expanders. The time control shows $\sqrt t\, \Sigma $, $t>0$; the $t=0$ view shows the nonregular initial cone only. 16898F334139 (Regular expanding trees with prescribed rays) A regular planar network consists of smooth branches meeting only at triple junctions, with angles $120$ degrees at every junction. title: 4.7 Mountain-pass self-expanders
text: 1EA720390291 Let $2\leq n\leq 6$, let $C\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a $C^3$-regular cone, and suppose two distinct strictly stable $C^2$-asymptotically conical self-expanders $\Gamma _-\preceq \Gamma _+$ approach $C$. The order means inclusion of their consistently oriented enclosed regions. Bernstein–Wang construct a further smooth properly embedded self-expander $\Gamma _0$ between them, meeting the open intervening region. The associated flow is $M_ t=\sqrt t\, \Gamma _0$, $t>0$, with $\mathbf H=X^\perp /2$. If the cone is generic in the precise sense that every expander asymptotic to it has no nontrivial Jacobi field fixing infinity, $\Gamma _0$ can be chosen unstable for expander weighted area. The theorem does not prescribe its genus, connectedness, symmetry or uniqueness. Completeness follows from proper embeddedness without boundary. Cone asymptotics give Euclidean area growth and hence finite Gaussian area and entropy; no numerical value is supplied. Corollary 1.3 gives an open set of cones admitting at least two connected and one disconnected smoothing, beyond the rotational setting. Sources: [ BWMP20 ] , Theorem 1.1 and Corollaries 1.2–1.3, pp. 1–2. In higher dimensions the general theorem allows a singular set of codimension seven; only its smooth $2\leq n\leq 6$ cases are catalogued here. title: 4.8 Expanders of unbounded genus at a fixed cone
search_title: Expanders of unbounded genus at a fixed cone
section: 4.8 Expanders of unbounded genus at a fixed cone
text: 3A8C3B21B572 Hoffman–Martín–White construct connected embedded self-expanders in $\mathbb R^3$ of arbitrarily large genus at a single suitable cone. Precisely, let $C=C_ k$ satisfy the symmetry and three-component link hypotheses of their Theorem 1.1, with its spherical link sufficiently close to the equatorial plane as required in Theorem 1.2. For each odd prime $p$ and integer $a\geq 0$, there are at least four noncongruent $G_ k$-invariant expanders asymptotic to $C$, of genus $p^ a k-1$. These are complete proper noncompact surfaces with three conical ends; the end count follows from the three components of the link. They solve $\mathbf H=X^\perp /2$ and yield $\sqrt t\, E$ for $t>0$. They are obtained by degree theory and limiting constructions, not an explicit formula. No common convexity, stability, or numerical entropy value is asserted. Smooth conical ends imply finite Gaussian area and entropy. The incoming shrinker $M_ k$ has genus $2k-2$. Joining $\sqrt{-t}\, M_ k$ for $t<0$, $C$ at $t=0$, and $\sqrt t\, E$ for $t>0$ gives the source's self-similar Brakke flow, smooth except at the spacetime origin. This is not a genus increase in a smooth flow across $t=0$. Source: [ HMWExpand26 ] , Theorems 1.1–1.2 and equation (1.5), pp. 2–3. The figure is an original topology model, not a numerical solution of the expander equation. The three ends wrap around the $z$-axis, rather than forming three separate tubes. Its displayed cone and small symmetry counts are illustrative; they are not asserted to be the cone $C_ k$ of a constructed shrinker or to satisfy the theorem's quantitative hypotheses. The two slice pairings follow Definition 3.1 and Figure 1 (pp. 9–10): in the reflection plane $\{ y=0\} $, the middle end on the positive-$x$ side is joined to the upper end for type 1, and to the lower end for type 2, with no closed slice curves. Each type has both a small and a big expander. These terms refer to the local integral $\int _ E\phi \, d\mathcal H^2$, below or above the threshold $3/2$, where $\phi $ is a fixed nonnegative radial function supported in $B(0,1/2)$ and normalized by $\int _{\{ z=0\} }\phi \, d\mathcal H^2=1$ (Definition 4.1 and Theorem 4.3). They do not refer to the magnification of the picture. Theorem 5.1 (p. 12) gives all four classes, and Theorems 12.6–12.7 (pp. 39–40) retain genus and class when the boundary radius tends to infinity. 3A8C3B21B572 Hoffman–Martín–White construct connected embedded self-expanders in $\mathbb R^3$ of arbitrarily large genus at a single suitable cone. title: 4.9 Knotted self-expanders
text: DA3FCE2F354F Mramor–Shengwen Wang construct complete properly embedded self-expanders in $\mathbb R^3$ with knotted topology. Their Theorem 3.1 starts with an embedded orientable surface bounding a handlebody and, with sufficiently many ends, produces an expander whose bounded-region topology realizes that handlebody. These surfaces are stable for the weighted functional $\int e^{|X|^2/4}\, d\mu $; this is expander weighted stability, not entropy stability. A concrete case has genus one and three ends: inside large balls it is isotopic to the boundary of a tubular neighborhood of a trefoil knot with three disks removed and annular ends attached. The half-cylinders in this description specify topology; the constructed geometric ends are asymptotically conical. More generally, every genus $g\geq 1$ occurs with sufficiently many ends, without a universal end count specified here. The normalization is $\mathbf H=X^\perp /2$, with flow $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M$ for $t>0$. The examples are noncompact, complete and proper. No explicit formula, uniqueness, or exact Gaussian-area or entropy value is provided; conical area growth gives finiteness. Source: [ MWKnotted26 ] , Theorems 1.1 and 3.1 and Corollary 3.2, pp. 2 and 8–10, arXiv v1 (November 2, 2026). This is a preprint construction, not independently verified here. The interactive picture shows a trefoil tube with three annular ends, with auxiliary views of the closed tube and its three punctures. The accompanying plate explains these topological operations; Figure 2 of the paper motivates the bridge description. All displayed shapes are schematics, not computed expanders. title: 5.4 The catenoid as an eternal stationary flow
search_title: The catenoid as an eternal stationary flow
section: 5.4 The catenoid as an eternal stationary flow
text: AC1C0D984A58 (Stationary catenoid flow) For $a>0$ the explicit immersion \[  X(\theta ,s,t)=a(\cosh s\cos \theta ,\cosh s\sin \theta ,s), \quad \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z,\quad s\in \mathbb R,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] is independent of time and has $\vec H=0$. It is therefore an eternal stationary mean curvature flow in $\mathbb R^3$. Every time slice is a complete properly embedded noncompact rotational annulus, with two ends and a waist circle of radius $a$. Its metric and curvature are \[  g=a^2\cosh ^2s(d\theta ^2+ds^2),\qquad K=-\frac1{a^2\cosh ^4s},\qquad \int K\, dA=-4\pi .  \] The metric follows by differentiation, and the conformal curvature formula gives $K$ and its integral. The complete catenoid is unstable for compactly supported area variations: for a test function $f(s)$ independent of $\theta $, its second variation is \[  Q(f,f)=2\pi \int _{\mathbb R}\bigl ((f')^2-2\operatorname {sech}^2s\, f^2\bigr )\, ds.  \] Taking $f$ equal to one on $[-R,R]$, zero outside $[-2R,2R]$, and $|f'|\leq C/R$ makes this negative for large $R$. Each open half is a minimal graph over $r>a$, with $z=\pm a\operatorname {arcosh}(r/a)$, so it is stable for compactly supported variations in that half. These are minimal-area stability assertions, not a classification of dynamical stability under MCF. The supplied source also records the catenoid in [ Man11 ] , Remark 4.4.7, printed p. 105, supplied PDF p. 116. The parametrization is exact and supports interactive rotation, scale selection, and a truncated height range with the omitted infinite ends stated. title: 5.11 Mean curvature evolution of the Whitney sphere
search_title: Mean curvature evolution of the Whitney sphere
section: 5.11 Mean curvature evolution of the Whitney sphere
text: 245DFF2BED27 (A collapsing Lagrangian immersed sphere) For $n\geq 2$, the initial Whitney immersion in $\mathbb R^{2n}=\mathbb C^ n$ is explicitly \[  F_0(x_1,\ldots ,x_{n+1}) =\frac{(x_1,x_1x_{n+1},\ldots ,x_ n,x_ nx_{n+1})}{1+x_{n+1}^2}, \qquad (x_1,\ldots ,x_{n+1})\in S^ n.  \] It is a compact Lagrangian immersion, of dimension and codimension $n$, with one transverse double image point at the origin coming from the two poles. It is complete and proper as an immersion of a compact domain, and it is not embedded. Its equivariance reduces the geometry to the planar initial profile \[  \gamma _0(u)=\left(\frac{\sin u}{1+\cos ^2u}, \frac{\sin u\cos u}{1+\cos ^2u}\right), \qquad u\in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z.  \] For $n\geq 2$ the profile evolution is the equivariant equation \[  (\partial _ t\gamma )^\perp =\vec k-(n-1)\frac{\gamma ^\perp }{|\gamma |^2},  \] interpreted by the smooth equivariant immersion at the double point. It is not ordinary planar curve shortening. The maximal smooth mean curvature flow $F_ t$, $t\in [0,T)$, remains Lagrangian and equivariant. It collapses to the origin in finite time, and its tangent flow there is a Lagrangian plane with multiplicity two. The Whitney sphere is not a self-similar solution. These statements are the special case stated in [ Viana18 ] , pp. 1–3, especially the result on p. 2 and Theorem 1.3 on p. 3. The formulas above specify the initial geometry and its reduced equation, not a closed expression for $F_ t$ at positive time. The illustration specializes to $n=2$. Write $\gamma _ t=a+ib$. A single right-hand lobe, from one preimage of the origin to the other, generates the immersed two-sphere by \[  F_ t(u,v)=(\gamma _ t(u)\cos v,\gamma _ t(u)\sin v)\in \mathbb C^2, \qquad v\in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z.  \] The circles at the two endpoints collapse to the two distinct poles of the domain, which have the same image at the origin. Using both antipodal lobes would cover the same sphere twice. The time sequence pairs this surface, linearly projected from $\mathbb R^4$ to $\mathbb R^3$, with its planar profile. At $t=0$ the geometry is exact; the positive-time frames are numerical approximations of the equivariant PDE for $n=2$, with $\partial _ tF=\vec H$ and the initial scale fixed above. They show $0\leq t\leq 0.09$ on a common spatial scale, with no normalization by an estimated extinction time. The computation stops before the singularity: $0.09$ is not asserted to equal $T$. Spatial mesh refinement and tighter time-integration tolerances are compared, but these checks are not certified error bounds. The profile narrows and contracts rather than shrinking by a single scale factor. Its double point remains at the origin; further overlaps in the surface projection need not be intersections in $\mathbb R^4$. It is complete and proper as an immersion of a compact domain, and it is not embedded. The profile narrows and contracts rather than shrinking by a single scale factor. Its double point remains at the origin; further overlaps in the surface projection need not be intersections in $\mathbb R^4$. The multiplicity-two tangent plane is a parabolic blow-up limit, not an unscaled final surface displayed by the animation.

title: 5.5 Rotational degenerate neckpinch solutions
text: 922034E946EB (Angenent–Velázquez type-II singularities) Let $n\geq 2$, let $m\geq 3$ be odd, and let $K>0$. Choose a compact rotational target hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, smooth away from a cusp at the origin, whose radius satisfies $u_*(x)\sim \sqrt K\, x^{m/2}$ as $x\downarrow 0$ and whose other tip closes smoothly. Angenent and Velázquez construct smooth compact rotational mean curvature flows \[  M_ t=\{ (x,u(x,t)\omega ):a(t)\leq x\leq b(t),\  \omega \in S^{n-1}\} , \qquad t_0<t<T,  \] with smooth caps and positive radius between them. Each regular slice is an embedded sphere, hence complete and proper. The constructed flows remain close to the chosen target outside a small neighborhood of the origin as the construction interval is shortened. They are not supplied as ancient solutions or as solitons, and no closed formula for $u(x,t)$ is given. Set $\xi _*=(2(n-1)/K)^{1/m}$. At the left tip, \[  a(t)=-(\xi _*+o(1))(T-t)^{1/m},\qquad |\vec H|_{\rm tip}(t)=\left(\frac{\xi _*}{m}+o(1)\right)(T-t)^{1/m-1}.  \] Here the curvature coefficient is for the trace mean curvature, equivalently the magnitude $|\vec H|$ at this convex tip. Rotational smoothness makes the $n$ principal curvatures equal at the tip, so $|A|_{\rm tip}=|\vec H|_{\rm tip}/\sqrt n$. The maximum of $|A|$ is attained there; its blow-up rate is type II. The parabolic rescalings at the origin converge smoothly on compact sets to $S^{n-1}_{\sqrt{2(n-1)}}\times \mathbb R$, whereas rescaling about the tip by $A_{\max }(t)=\max _{M_ t}|A|$ yields the rotational translating bowl with tip $|A|=1$. This last normalization has translation speed $\sqrt n$; rescaling instead by $|\vec H|_{\rm tip}$ gives the speed-one bowl. Under the intermediate scaling $x\mapsto x/(T-t)^{1/m}$ and $r\mapsto r/(T-t)^{1/2}$, the limiting profile is \[  r=\sqrt{2(n-1)+Kx^ m},\qquad x\geq -\xi _*.  \] This last expression is an asymptotic limiting profile, not an exact formula for the evolving compact hypersurface. Source: [ AV97 ] , Introduction, items 1–5, printed pp. 16–17, supplied PDF pp. 2–3; the construction is justified in Sections 3–7. The even-$m$ modifications and the formal $m=2$ discussion are not included in this entry. The illustration selects $n=2$, $m=3$, $K=1$, and writes $s=T-t$. Its time sequence uses one spatial scale to show the left tip approaching the origin while the outer cap persists; the final cusp target is not a smooth time slice. For the profile near the origin, item 5 of the Introduction gives \[  \frac{u(y\sqrt{s},T-s)}{\sqrt{s}} =\sqrt{2}+\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2\sqrt{2}}(y^3-6y)+o(\sqrt{s})  \] on bounded $y$ intervals. This leading Hermite correction explains the small bulge and neck in the cylindrical region. The rotatable compact slices blend the asymptotic profiles with a numerically integrated bowl cap and a chosen outer cap: they are illustrative schematics, not a computed solution of the compact MCF initial-value problem, and their displayed times carry no certified finite-time accuracy. Separate views compare the meridians and the three blow-up limits; the intermediate view uses unequal axial and radial scaling. title: 5.1 The Angenent oval as an explicit ancient flow
search_title: The Angenent oval as an explicit ancient flow
section: 5.1 The Angenent oval as an explicit ancient flow
text: B008243C5D96 (The ancient paperclip curve) With the speed-one curve-shortening convention, the exact implicit equation \[  \Gamma _ t=\{ (x,y)\in \mathbb R^2:|x|<\pi /2,\  e^ t\cosh y=\cos x\} , \qquad -\infty <t<0,  \] defines the Angenent oval. Equivalently, its two graph branches are \[  y=\pm \operatorname {arcosh}(e^{-t}\cos x), \qquad |x|\leq \arccos (e^ t).  \] Their endpoints join smoothly as a curve, even though those graph charts cease to be regular there. This is an exact implicit formula, rather than a single global graph parametrization. It is recorded in [ BV11 ] , Section 3.1, equation (14), p. 7. Every time slice is a smooth compact embedded strictly convex curve, hence complete and proper, with topology $S^1$ and reflection symmetries across both coordinate axes. It shrinks to the origin at time zero but changes shape and is not a soliton. Its enclosed area is $-2\pi t$, and \[  \kappa _{\max }=(1-e^{2t})^{-1/2},\qquad \kappa _{\min }=e^ t(1-e^{2t})^{-1/2}.  \] The rescaling $(-t)^{-1/2}\Gamma _ t$ converges smoothly to the radius-$\sqrt2$ circle at extinction. As $t\to -\infty $, translating its upper and lower branches to keep their tips fixed gives the two oppositely directed grim-reaper profiles, locally in $|x|<\pi /2$. These limits can be read from the implicit equation: near extinction its quadratic expansion gives $x^2+y^2\sim -2t$, and subtracting the upper tip height gives the limiting graph $\log \cos x$ as $t\to -\infty $. The time slider plots the exact implicit curve for $-5\leq t\leq -0.1$ on a fixed spatial scale.
